underdiagnosed due to its subclinical nature and the challenges involved
in detecting carriers within the genital tract (Martins and Lilenbaum,
2017).
The primary causative agents of bovine leptospirosis are strains from
the Sejroe serogroup, which are noted for their adaptability to cattle.
Specifically, key genotypes implicated in bovine leptospirosis include
Hardjoprajitno (L. interrogans) and Hardjobovis (L. borgpetersenii) (Ellis,
2015). Experimental studies conducted over the past decades have
demonstrated the interaction of these genotypes with bovine hosts
(Bercovich et al., 1990; Leonard et al., 1992; Cortese et al., 2007; Rocha
et al., 2020; Wilson-Welder et al., 2021), showing that infection by these
strains can induce reproductive disease. Hardjoprajitno has been
frequently reported in Europe and Brazil (Ellis, 2015; Cosate et al., 2015;
Aym´ee et al., 2023a), while Hardjobovis has been identified as the
predominant agent of bovine leptospirosis in North America (Putz et al.,
2022). Another emerging agent within the Sejroe serogroup is Guaricura
(L. santarosai), increasingly reported in Latin America and also associ-
ated with reproductive disease (Aym´ee et al., 2022a; Chinchilla et al.,
2023). However, these conclusions are primarily based on leptospiral
isolation and serological studies, with limited genetic characterization.
Furthermore, most studies focus on diagnosis, while related epidemio-
logical aspects remain sparse or absent.
Serology serves as an indirect diagnostic method based on the host’s
production of specific antibodies, providing epidemiological insights
into circulating serogroups within specific herds or regions (Aym´ee
et al., 2024). While useful for collective diagnosis, serology has limita-
tions, particularly in identifying subclinical infections characterized by
low antibody titers in individuals. In contrast, molecular diagnosis via
polymerase chain reaction (PCR) offers a direct approach to detect
carriers and circulating genotypes. Discrepancies often arise between
serological and molecular results, with many seronegative animals
testing positive by PCR, highlighting the need for complementary mo-
lecular tools alongside serology (Pinna et al., 2018; Di Azevedo and
Lilenbaum, 2021).
Due to the host-adapted interaction between Sejroe serogroup lep-
tospires and bovines, the disease typically manifests chronically, char-
acterized by infertility, birth of weak calves, repeated estrus, and
pregnancy losses (Aym´ee et al., 2024). Leptospires can colonize the
kidneys or genital tract of cattle for extended periods and are shed in
body fluids such as urine, cervicovaginal mucus, and semen. In the
environment, these bacteria infect susceptible animals through mucous
membranes (Loureiro and Lilenbaum, 2020).
Historically, kidneys have been the primary focus of Leptospira spp.
colonization studies (Hern´andez-Rodríguez et al., 2011; Guedes et al.,
2021; Saglam et al., 2022). However, recent research has shed light on
genital tract infections by Sejroe strains, which have been identified in
the uterus (Aym´ee et al., 2022b; Di Azevedo et al., 2020), follicular fluid
(Di Azevedo et al., 2021; Pereira et al., 2022), cervicovaginal mucus
(Loureiro et al., 2016; Pimenta et al., 2019; Gonçalves et al., 2021), and
semen (Vinodh et al., 2008). Notably, studies in a hamster model
demonstrated that Sejroe leptospires exhibit a preference for the uterus
over other immunologically privileged sites like the kidneys (Pinto et al.,
2020). Chronic genital infection by leptospires is now recognized as
Bovine Genital Leptospirosis (BGL) (Loureiro and Lilenbaum, 2020).
Recent investigations in South America have linked Leptospira spp.
serogroup Sejroe to infertility and subtle reproductive signs (Macchi
et al., 2024; Oliveira et al., 2021; Libonati et al., 2018), further
emphasizing the significance of these strains in chronic bovine
leptospirosis.
Many naturally infected cows have been identified carrying Sejroe
strains in their genital tracts, with a high incidence of reproductive
failures observed among these animals. Despite the availability of a
substantial sequence bank for Leptospira spp. identified in cattle world-
wide, there has been a notable absence of elucidative and comparative
studies based on genetically characterized strains. Therefore, the current
study aimed to conduct genetic typing of Leptospira spp. strains
belonging to serogroup Sejroe, using sequences obtained from isolates
and clinical samples, in order to assess the genetic diversity of these
strains based on their geographical origin and anatomical site of infec-
tion through in silico methods. The overarching goal of the research was
to provide crucial epidemiological insights into this silent yet neglected
disease.
2. Material and methods
To improve the number of sequences of Leptospira spp. from genital
samples of bovines with a history of reproductive problems, we first
performed field sampling, followed by molecular diagnosis and genetic
characterization. The study was approved by the Ethical Committee for
Animal Use of Federal Fluminense University under protocol number
9527220222.
2.1. Animal specimens, sample collection, and molecular diagnosis
A total of 47 non-pregnant cows from two herds in Southeastern
Brazil with poor reproductive profiles were selected based on their
history of reproductive failures. Herd #1 was located in Araruama
municipality, Rio de Janeiro State, and comprised Tabapu˜a and Nelore
beef cattle aged between 3 and 10 years. The second herd (Herd #2) was
situated in Coronel Pacheco municipality, Minas Gerais State, and
consisted of Holstein dairy cows aged between 3 and 5 years. Geore-
ferencing was conducted using a portable GPS.
Cows from both herds exhibited a history of chronic subfertility/
infertility, embryonic death, and abortions. Each of the 47 cows (41
from Herd #1 and 6 from Herd #2) underwent sampling of uterine
fragments (UF) and cervicovaginal mucus (CVM) following procedures
recommended by Aym´ee and colleagues (2021). All 47 UF and 47 CVM
samples were processed for DNA extraction using the DNeasy® Blood &
Tissue Kit (Qiagen, California, USA) following the manufacturer’s
instructions.
For the detection of pathogenic Leptospira spp., PCR based on the
lipL32 gene was performed as described by Hamond et al. (2014). Each
sample set included ultrapure water as a negative control in all re-
actions, and 10fg of DNA extracted from Leptospira interrogans serovar
Copenhageni (Fiocruz L1–130) served as a positive control. The PCR
products were analyzed by electrophoresis in a 1.5–2 % agarose gel and
visualized under ultraviolet light after staining with GelRed®.
2.2. Genetic characterization of pathogenic Leptospira spp.
Samples positive in lipL32-PCR were submitted for Single Locus
Sequence Typing (SLST) based on the secY gene, already well described
in the literature as an efficient genetic marker of the Leptospira genus
(Lam et al., 2020). A nested PCR was conducted, with an initial reaction
using the primers secY_outerF (5′-ATGCCGATCATTTTTGCTTC-3′) and
secY_outerR (5′-CCGTCCCTTAATTTTAGACTTCTTC-3′), followed by a
second reaction with the amplicons using the primers secY_inner_F
(5′-CCTCAGACGATTATTCAATGGTTATC-3′) and secY_inner_R
(5′-AGAAGAGAAGTTCCACCGAATG-3′) (Grillov´a et al., 2020). Gel
electrophoresis and amplicons’ revelation followed the same procedures
described above for lipL32-PCR.
The amplicons were purified using the PCR Clean-Up System Kit
(Promega, USA), following the manufacturer’s instructions, and pre-
pared for sequencing. Sequencing reactions were performed using the
Big Dye Terminator v Kit. 3.1 Cycle Sequencing (Applied Biosystems,
USA) on a 3100 automatic DNA sequencer according to the manufac-
turer’s instructions. The Basic Local Alignment Search Tool (BLAST -
NCBI, https://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/Blast) was used to initially iden-
tify Leptospira species based on nucleotide similarity.

2.3. In silico analysis - phylogenetic reconstruction and genetic diversity
evaluation
The sequences obtained from the present study were subjected to an
in silico analysis for phylogenetic reconstruction and genetic diversity
evaluation. To enrich molecular epidemiological inferences, secY se-
quences of Leptospira spp. available in GenBank were selected globally.
Inclusion criteria encompassed: i) sequences identified as belonging to
the Sejroe serogroup (either by serological characterization or high
sequence identity); ii) sequences exceeding 400 bp in length; iii) se-
quences associated with published articles.
SeqMan DNASTAR v. 7.0 (Inc., Madison, WI, USA) and BioEdit v.
7.0.1 (Hall, 1999) were employed for sequence editing and analysis.
Sequences were aligned using ClustalX v 2.0 software (Larkin et al.,
2007), and a maximum likelihood (ML) tree was constructed in MEGA X
software (Kumar et al., 2018). The most appropriate DNA substitution
model was determined using the Bayesian information criterion. Genetic
distances were computed in MEGA X with the selected model based on
the dataset. The saprophytic species Leptospira biflexa strain Patoc served
as an outgroup.
To assess haplotype distribution according to the anatomical site of
infection, a haplotype network was constructed using the median-
joining inference method (Bandelt et al., 1999) with the population
genetics software PopART (Leigh and Bryant, 2015).
3. Results
3.1. Molecular diagnosis and history of herds with reproductive disorders
Of the 47 animals sampled, 32 (68.0 %) tested positive for lipL32-
PCR, regardless of the analyzed sample. Of these PCR-positive cows, 10
(31.3 %) were positive only in CVM samples, six (18.7 %) were positive
only in UF, and 16 (50.0 %) were positive in both CVM and UF. Of the
positive animals, chronic infertility and embryonic mortality were the
most commonly reported signs observed in 26/47 (55.3 %) and 23/47
(48.9 %) cows, respectively. Abortions were less frequent and were re-
ported in only 6/47 (12.7 %) animals.
3.2. Genetic characterization of pathogenic Leptospira spp.
Based on the secY gene, it was possible to sequence nine Leptospira
spp. amplicons (409 bp) from cervicovaginal mucus (n=2) and uterine
fragment (n=7) (Table 1). The sequences obtained in this study have
been deposited in GenBank under accession numbers OR611992 to
OR612000. After Pairwise/ Blast/NCBI comparisons with the GenBank
secY gene dataset, all sequences were identified as L. interrogans with an
identity > 99 %. Furthermore, sequences from the present study
exhibited high identity (>99 %) with reference strains from the Sejroe
serogroup (Norma and L53).
3.3. In silico analysis of Leptospira spp. sequences from Sejroe serogroup
3.3.1. Sequences from previous studies obtained from GenBank
In addition to the nine sequences from the present study, 108 se-
quences from GenBank met the inclusion criteria, resulting in a total of
117 sequences for further analysis (Table 1). The majority of sequences
belonged to L. borgpetersenii genotype Hardjobovis (50.4 %), followed by
L. interrogans genotype Hardjoprajitno (41 %) and L. santarosai serovar
Guaricura (8.6 %). These sequences originated from animals in four
different countries across three continents: Brazil (69.2 %), Tanzania
(12.8 %), the USA (9.4 %), and Uruguay (8.5 %). Regarding the site of
collection, the majority of genetically characterized Leptospira spp. were
of renal origin (n=66, 56.4 %), including 24 from kidneys and 42 from
urines, while 43.6 % were from genital sites (n=51), comprising 30
uterine fragments (UF), 10 cervicovaginal mucus (CVM), and 11 follic-
ular fluids. From the obtained sequences, clinical history information
was available for 43.5 % (51/117). Among these cases, chronic sub-
fertility (64.7 %), abortion (33.3 %), and embryonic mortality (41.2 %)
were commonly reported. In the remaining cases, cows were described
as asymptomatic (21.6 %). Table 2 summarizes all these results.
3.3.2. Phylogenetic reconstruction
The ML phylogenetic tree was constructed using the Tamura 3-
parameter (TN92) model, which was identified as the most suitable
DNA substitution model. Together with reference sequences, the ML-
TN92 tree confirmed the species identification of sequences from the
present study (CVM56, CVM62, UT63, UT64, UT67, UT72, UT83, UT90,
UT100). These sequences formed a maximum-supported clade (boot-
strap = 100 %) with L. interrogans sequences, distinct from other com-
mon species found in bovines (Fig. 1). Furthermore, sequences from the
present study clustered together in a large haplogroup predominantly
comprising sequences from the same geographical origin in south and
southeast Brazil (Group B in Fig. 1; Table 1). Additionally, two other
major haplogroups, A and C, were identified within L. interrogans,
encompassing 9 and 13 sequences, respectively.
Based on the inclusion criteria, L. interrogans and L. santarosai were
exclusively identified in bovines from Brazil, while L. borgpetersenii was
also found in the USA, Tanzania, and Uruguay (Fig. 1). Notably, despite
originating from different geographic locations, a larger haplogroup
consisting of 52 sequences was observed in L. borgpetersenii, whereas a
smaller haplogroup was exclusively composed of strains from Tanzania
(n=9). Moreover, the majority of L. borgpetersenii sequences from Brazil
originated from the Amazon region (North) (Table 1).
In terms of intraspecific genetic distances (TN92±SD), L. interrogans
and L. borgpetersenii exhibited low diversity with 0.01±0.00 (99 %
identity between sequences), whereas L. santarosai showed higher
intraspecific diversity with a distance of 0.03±0.01 (97 % identity). This
diversity in L. santarosai resulted in the formation of small haplogroups,
each comprising a maximum of three strains (Fig. 1).
Regarding the geographic distribution of Sejroe strains, high intra-
and interspecific diversity was observed in Brazil. In contrast, homo-
geneous populations were noted in other countries such as the USA and
Tanzania. Additionally, an exclusive haplogroup was identified in
L. borgpetersenii from Tanzania (Fig. 1).
3.3.3. Haplotype network of L. interrogans
To analyze the distribution of haplotypes based on the site of infec-
tion (renal vs. genital), a haplotype network was constructed using
L. interrogans secY sequences, which included a significant number of
genital samples (n=44) in addition to renal samples (n=4). Three main
haplogroups (A, B, and C) were identified.
Notably, haplogroups B and C exclusively comprised L. interrogans
strains originating from genital sources, including cervicovaginal mucus
(CVM) and uterine fragments (UF). In contrast, haplogroup A included
strains isolated from renal sources and follicular fluid. Specifically,
haplogroup B contained sequences from both CVM and UF, whereas
haplogroup C consisted solely of sequences from UF (Fig. 2).
4. Discussion
The present study focused on gathering and genetically analyzing
leptospiral Sejroe strains from cows to enhance understanding of
chronic bovine leptospirosis. In addition to sequences from previous
studies, our research contributed nine new sequences from genital
samples, enriching the phylogenetic analysis and yielding notable
findings.
We observed a high prevalence of PCR-positive animals among the
herds studied. Most of the 47 non-pregnant cows exhibited subclinical
symptoms such as chronic infertility and embryonic death, with a
smaller number experiencing abortions. This aligns with previous re-
ports linking bovine leptospirosis to embryonic death leading to estrus
repetitions and abortions in cattle herds (Libonati et al., 2018; Oliveira

et al., 2021; Aym´ee et al., 2023b). The frequent occurrence of chronic
subfertility/infertility and embryonic deaths underscores the silent na-
ture of leptospirosis in cattle, complicating diagnosis and contributing to
its underestimation. Based on these findings, we emphasize the
importance of a diagnostic flowchart proposed for identifying the silent
chronic form of animal leptospirosis. This approach involves initial
serological screening of herds followed by individual molecular testing
using lipL32-PCR on genital samples, complemented by secY gene
sequencing, which provides reliable taxonomic resolution (Di Azevedo
and Lilenbaum, 2021).
In this study, we successfully amplified and sequenced nine samples
based on the secY gene, which represents a smaller number compared to
the amplicons obtained from lipL32-PCR. This difference can be attrib-
uted to the smaller size of the lipL32 fragment (242 bp) relative to the
secY amplicon (409 bp), making the amplification of the smaller region
more reliable in clinical samples where bacterial DNA quantity and
quality may be suboptimal.
All genital secY sequences identified in our study were characterized
as L. interrogans with high identity to Sejroe strains, consistent with
previous findings reporting the presence of this pathogenic Leptospira
spp. in the region (Di Azevedo et al., 2021; Aym´ee et al., 2021; Pereira
et al., 2022). For a broader epidemiological overview, we included 108
sequences from GenBank, combined with our nine sequences, totaling
117 sequences for phylogenetic analysis. The predominant species
identified were L. borgpetersenii and L. interrogans, known as key agents
of bovine leptospirosis globally, particularly in countries like the United
States and Uruguay, where their presence is frequently detected using
molecular methods or culturing of urine and kidney samples

L. santarosai, considered an emerging pathogen in the Americas, was
also identified, particularly associated with serogroup Sejroe and iso-
lated from both genital and urinary tracts (Aym´ee et al., 2022a).
Therefore, the presence of these three species in association with Sejroe
strains in cattle was anticipated.
The phylogenetic analysis revealed multiple distinct clades of Lep-
tospira spp. associated with chronic bovine leptospirosis (see Fig. 1). The
presence of different bacterial clades causing similar pathogenesis in the
same reservoirs suggests mechanisms such as mutations, genetic
recombination, or horizontal gene transfer may be at play. The intricate
epidemiological cycle of leptospires, involving diverse hosts and
ecological niches, likely contributes to their emergence and adaptability
under different selective pressures. This pattern of convergent evolution
underscores the complex interplay between microbial evolution, host
immune responses, and environmental factors (Didelot et al., 2016).
Over the past decades, Brazil has led genetic characterization studies
of bovine leptospirosis targeting the secY gene, resulting in the country
having the largest repository of sequences. However, there remains a
notable absence of molecular characterization of Leptospira spp. from
genital samples in countries outside Brazil, which explains the
predominance of renal samples in global studies. This gap underscores
the critical need for new research initiatives focusing on the genital site
in diverse geographical regions.
Moreover, many associated studies have not provided detailed
reproductive histories of the animals, limiting the ability to draw
comprehensive inferences about the disease. The lack of association
between infection and clinical signs may stem from studies conducted in
slaughterhouses or the subtle manifestations of the disease, which can
easily go unnoticed in field settings.
It is important to note that while L. interrogans and L. santarosai are
exclusively reported in Brazil, their absence in other countries cannot be
definitively concluded due to the lack of available secY sequences
meeting inclusion criteria. The genetic studies of leptospires suffer from
a lack of standardization in the genetic markers used, which hampers
comprehensive molecular epidemiological investigations. To mitigate
this issue, we advocate for the widespread adoption of the secY gene,
recognized for its efficacy in defining genomic species and assessing
intraspecific diversity (Lam et al., 2020).
The sequences from our study exhibited high similarity with refer-
ence strains from the Sejroe serogroup (Norma and L53), and the ML-

other strains from the same region (Fig. 1; Table 1). This finding re-
inforces the epidemiological significance of L. interrogans in south-
eastern Brazil. Conversely, in northern Brazil, L. borgpetersenii
predominates, particularly identified from urinary tract samples
(Guedes et al., 2020; et al., 2021), with no investigations on genital
samples reported.
The genotype Hardjobovis (L. borgpetersenii) is known to be more
associated with host-host interactions, whereas Hardjoprajitno
(L. interrogans) is often linked to environmental transmission due to its
enhanced environmental resilience. The distinct climatic conditions,
rainfall patterns, vegetation types, and interspecies interactions in the
Amazon (northern Brazil) versus the Atlantic Forest (southeastern
Brazil) biomes likely contribute to these contrasting results. Further
studies are imperative to elucidate the influence of biome-specific fac-
tors on the distribution and diversity of Leptospira spp. genotypes.
The phylogenetic analysis in our study highlighted the genetic sim-
ilarity among L. borgpetersenii strains regardless of their geographical
origin, which may be attributed to the species’ smaller genome size and
potentially reduced genetic diversity (Bulach et al., 2006). This char-
acteristic suggests that L. borgpetersenii strains may primarily transmit
through direct animal-animal contact rather than persisting in diverse
environmental sources.
Our findings suggest that L. borgpetersenii genotype Hardjobovis
tends to favor colonization of the urinary tract, while L. interrogans ge-
notype Hardjoprajitno appears more associated with the genital tract.
However, further investigations specifically targeting the genital tract
are essential to elucidate why certain strains exhibit a preference for
different anatomical sites.
Regarding L. santarosai, our study and others have observed high
genomic diversity within this species, reflecting its adaptability and
emergence in Latin America. It has been isolated from various sources,
including urine, vaginal fluid, and uterus, associated particularly with
serovar Guaricura (Loureiro et al., 2016). These observations underscore
the dynamic nature of L. santarosai and its potential impact on bovine
health.
A notable outcome of our study is the distinct haplotype distribution
observed in the L. interrogans phylogenetic network. Haplogroups A, B,
and C delineate strains from urinary and genital origins, with B and C
exclusively associated with genital strains. These findings underscore
significant differences between strains colonizing the genital and renal
sites. Although experimentally demonstrated (Pinto et al., 2020), the
complex host-pathogen relationship observed between cattle and Sejroe
strains remains unclear, and scientists have yet to elucidate why some
strains seem to have a predilection for urinary or genital colonization in
cows. More experimental and genomic studies are needed, and more
novel outcomes may offer important insights to address this gap in
understanding.
The study underscores the genital site as a crucial reservoir for
leptospiral infection in cattle, particularly associated with Bovine Gen-
ital Leptospirosis (BGL). It emphasizes the urgent need for clinical vet-
erinarians and researchers to prioritize the use of genital samples like
uterine fragments and cervical, vaginal mucus for accurate diagnosis,
aligning with the diagnostic protocol proposed by Aym´ee et al. (2023b).
Moreover, current vaccines against leptospirosis are based on inter-
national reference strains primarily isolated from the renal tract. Given
the distinct epidemiological role of genital strains in reproductive fail-
ures, there is uncertainty about the efficacy of these vaccines against
BGL. Therefore, our study advocates for research into vaccination using
locally adapted strains, ideally of genital origin, to enhance protection
against bovine leptospirosis and mitigate economic losses associated
with reproductive failures.
5. Conclusion
Herein, we have presented a groundbreaking molecular epidemio-
logical perspective on the primary causative agents of chronic bovine
leptospirosis, affirming that L. borgpetersenii genotype Hardjobovis and
L. interrogans genotype Hardjoprajitno are predominant circulating
strains. Importantly, our study has demonstrated that pathogenic lep-
tospires originating from genital sources cluster within an exclusive

This novel finding provides valuable insights into the distribution and
circulation patterns of pathogenic Leptospira spp. associated specifically
with chronic bovine leptospirosis. Furthermore, our results underscore
the potential benefits of developing vaccines composed of locally
adapted strains. Given the distinct epidemiological roles of genital
strains in bovine reproductive health, such vaccines could play a pivotal
role in enhancing prophylactic measures against bovine leptospirosis.
Continued research in this direction holds promise for improving disease
management and livestock health outcomes.

ARTIGO 3: Caracterização genética e potencial zoonótico de Leptospira
interrogans identificada em pequenos mamíferos n ão voadores da Mata
Atlântica Sudeste, Brasil
Revista: Tropical Medicine and Infectious Diseases (IF= 2.6)

A leptospirose é uma zoonose de importância global para a saúde pública,
causada por bactérias do gênero Leptospira. Pequenos mamíferos não voadores
são importantes reservatórios do patógeno. A Mata Atlântica B rasileira é um
hotspot de biodiversidade localizado em uma área densamente povoada e
sujeita a intensa degradação. Embora documentada por meio de inquéritos
sorológicos e da detecção de DNA de leptospiras em pequenos mamíferos
selvagens, nenhum estudo realizou a caracterização genética da bactéri a na
região. O presente estudo teve como objetivo avaliar a diversidade genética de
leptospiras patogênicas identificadas em pequenos mamíferos não voadores na
Mata Atlântica Sudeste e realizar inferências genéticas intraespecíficas com
outros hospedeiros. A área estudada incluiu cinco diferentes unidades de
conservação. O diagnóstico molecular foi realizado com base no gene lipl32. O
método de tipificação SLST foi aplicado com base no gene secY. No total, 56%
das amostras foram positivas na lipL32-PCR e identificadas como L. interrogans,
com alta identidade genética entre elas, distribuídas em quatro hapl ótipos
principais. O maior hapl ótipo também incluiu sequências de referência de
humanos, cães e ratos urbanos, todos pertencentes ao sorogrupo
Icterohaemorrhagiae. Nossos resultados reforçam o papel de pequenos
mamíferos como importantes portadores de L. interrogans e destacam a Mata
Atlântica como um ambiente significativo para a circulação e disseminação de
espiroquetas com potencial zoonótico.

Abstract: Leptospirosis is a zoonotic disease of global public health importance caused by
bacteria of the genus Leptospira. Small non-flying mammals are important reservoirs of the
pathogen. The Brazilian Atlantic Forest is a biodiversity hotspot located in a densely popu-
lated area and subject to intense degradation. Although documented through serosurveys
and the detection of leptospiral DNA in wild small mammals, no study has performed a
genetic characterization of the bacteria in the region. The present study aimed to evaluate
the genetic diversity of pathogenic leptospires identified in small non-flying mammals in
the Southeast Atlantic Forest and to perform intraspecific genetic inferences with other
hosts. The studied area included five different conservation units. Molecular diagnosis
was performed based on the lipl32 gene. The SLST typing method was applied based
on the secY gene. In total, 56% of samples were lipL32-PCR-positive and identified as L.
interrogans, with a high genetic identity among them, distributed in four main haplogroups.
The largest haplogroup also included reference sequences from humans, dogs, and urban
rats, all belonging to the Icterohaemorrhagiae serogroup. Our results reinforce the role of
small mammals as important carriers of L. interrogans and highlight the Atlantic Forest
as a significant environment for the circulation and dissemination of spirochetes with
zoonotic potential.
Keywords: leptospirosis; zoonosis; one health; Akodon; secY
1. Introduction
Leptospirosis is a globally neglected, reemerging zoonotic disease of global public
health importance caused by pathogenic spirochetal bacteria of the genus Leptospira that
circulates among a wide spectrum of hosts, including humans and domestic and wild
animals [1]. Leptospires can survive in the environment, particularly in moist conditions,
and can be transmitted through different routes: (i) direct contact with the urine of an
infected animal; (ii) indirect contact with contaminated water, soil, or feed; and (iii) sexual
and vertical transmission in some species (e.g., bovine) [2].
Historically, the etiology of leptospiral infections can be divided into those determined
by host-adapted or incidental strains [ 3]. Adapted strains are observed in the reservoir
Trop. Med. Infect. Dis. 2025, 10, 62 https://doi.org/10.3390/tropicalmed10030062

Trop. Med. Infect. Dis. 2025, 10, 62 2 of 11
animal host, resulting from a long process of host–pathogen coevolution, leading to asymp-
tomatic or inapparent disease or mild and subclinical symptoms of a chronic nature [ 3].
These maintenance hosts are infected asymptomatic animals that shed viable leptospires in
their fluids, acting simultaneously as hosts and reservoirs. They play an important role in
the epidemiology of leptospirosis, harboring and shedding leptospires in the environment
for long periods, becoming important sources of leptospiral infection for non-adapted
hosts [4]. Examples of adapted serovars are Bratislava in horses, Pomona in pigs, Hardjo in
ruminants, Canicola in dogs, and Icterohaemorrhagiae in rodents [5]. On the other hand,
incidental serovars infect hosts other than the maintenance ones, leading to an apparent
acute, often severe illness [4]. Importantly, the L. interrogans serogroup Icterohaemorrhagiae
is the most associated with acute human disease [6], highlighting the incidental nature of
infection in people.
The clinical signs of leptospirosis in humans and animals are diverse and can affect
multiple organ systems. In humans, the disease can present with a wide spectrum of symp-
toms, ranging from mild, flu-like symptoms to severe, life-threatening conditions such as
Weil’s disease, characterized by jaundice, renal failure, and hemorrhagic manifestations [7].
The bacteria enter through abrasions or cuts in the skin and mucous membranes, including
the conjunctiva [8]. Macerated skin, resulting from prolonged exposure to water, is also a
suspected route of infection [9].
Small non-flying mammals, such as rodents and marsupials, play a crucial role in the
epidemiology of leptospirosis and act as reservoirs of Leptospira spp. [8]. These animals
shed the bacteria in their urine, contaminating the environment, particularly water sources.
This can lead to human infection through direct or indirect contact with contaminated water
or soil, representing a constant risk, especially in urban and peri-urban environments [10].
Due to its high biodiversity and species endemism in a small remaining area, the
Brazilian Atlantic Forest is among the world’s 36 biodiversity hotspots [11]. It harbors a
wide range of mammalian hosts, which provide favorable biotic conditions for the bacterial
cycle. In addition, it is located in a tropical region and presents ideal environmental abiotic
conditions, such as a hot and humid climate, that favor the survival of leptospires [ 12].
Several wild and domestic animals live in the region, including 72% of the Brazilian
population [13]. Leptospirosis is endemic in this region, with an average of 3810 cases
reported annually and with higher numbers in urban areas, including the Rio de Janeiro
state, located in the southeastern region of the Atlantic Forest, where the disease remains a
significant public health concern, with periodic outbreaks, particularly during the rainy
season [14]. Poverty and urbanization, among other environmental and socioeconomic
factors, influence morbidity and mortality rates [15].
The few studies that have documented the occurrence of Leptospira spp. in small
mammals in the Atlantic Forest [16–19] were based on serosurveys, which present limited
value since reservoirs may not be detected by serology [20]. Previous studies conducted by
our group in the region have identified the presence of pathogenic leptospiral DNA in wild
marsupials and rodents based on conventional PCR [21,22]. However, to date, no study
has performed a genetic characterization of the bacteria.
Therefore, the present study aimed to analyze the genetic diversity of pathogenic lep-
tospires identified in small non-flying mammals in the Atlantic Forest of southeastern Brazil,
comparing the identified haplotypes with those described in human and domestic animals
to assess the risk of zoonotic transmission and provide new epidemiological inferences.

2.2. Molecular Diagnosis
All unprocessed small mammal kidney samples ( n = 139) were subjected to DNA
extraction using a DNeasy® Blood & Tissue Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany following the
manufacturer’s instructions. For detecting pathogenic Leptospira spp., lipL32 gene-based
PCR was performed using primers and conditions described by Hamond et al. (2014) [23].
Each sample set included ultrapure water as a negative control in all reactions, and 10fg of
DNA extracted from Leptospira interrogans serovar Copenhageni (Fiocruz L1–130) served
as a positive control. PCR products were analyzed by 2% agarose gel electrophoresis and
visualized under ultraviolet light after staining with GelRed®.
2.3. Genetic Characterization of Pathogenic Leptospira spp.
All samples positive for the lipL32 gene were subjected to a nested PCR based on the
secY gene, a genetic marker with good taxonomic resolution, whose use is well established
for the genetic characterization of leptospires [24]. Reactions were performed using primers
and conditions described in Grillová et al., 2020 [25], with the enzyme Platinum Taq DNA
Polymerase kit (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA). The amplicons were purified with a
PCR Clean-Up System Kit (Promega, Madison, WI, USA) according to the manufacturer’s
instructions and intended for sequencing. The reactions were performed in both directions
using a Big Dye Terminator v . 3.1 Cycle Sequencing Kit (Applied Biosystems, Foster City , CA,
USA) on a 3100 automated DNA sequencer according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
2.4. Phylogenetic Analyses
For molecular epidemiology purposes, we used the Single Locus Sequencing Typing
(SLST) typing method. For this, sequences of the secY gene were selected from GenBank
and subjected to phylogenetic analyses with the sequences obtained in the present study.
Very short sequences (<400 bp) were excluded to avoid bias. After aligning the sequences
in the ClustalX v 2.0 software [26], a maximum likelihood (ML) tree was constructed in
MEGA X software v 11.0.13 [27] using the best-fitting DNA substitution model determined
by the Bayesian information criterion. Genetic distances were calculated in MEGA X with
the model previously determined by the analysis of the data set.
2.5. Assessment of Genetic Diversity and Determination of Haplotype Circulation Patterns
The identification of unique haplotypes was performed after screening in the DAMBE
software v 7.3.32 [28]. To assess the intraspecific genetic diversity of Leptospira spp. pop-
ulations and evaluate the dynamics of haplotype circulation between different hosts and
regions, haplotype networks were constructed from the aligned sequences and scripts
in nexus format in the PopART population genetics software using the median-joining
inference method [29].
3. Results
3.1. Molecular Identification of Pathogenic Leptospira spp.
Of the 139 samples processed and submitted to molecular diagnosis based on the
lipL32 PCR, 78 (56%) were positive. Those 78 plus the 63 previously positive samples [21,22]
were subjected to a nested PCR based on thesecY genetic marker, totaling 141 DNA samples.
It was possible to obtain strong amplicons, suitable for sequencing, from 93 samples.
3.2. Genetic Characterization of Pathogenic Leptospira spp. Identified
Based on the secY gene sequencing, all samples were identified as L. interrogans with

3.3. Phylogenetic Analyses and Haplotype Distribution
The Tamura Nei model (TN92) was the best DNA substitution model determined.
Based on this, a high genetic identity was found among the sequences from the present
study (TN92 = 0.01± 0.01; 99% identity). The phylogenetic analyses and haplotype network
demonstrated the presence of four main haplogroups, Hap#1 (n = 68), Hap#2 (n = 9), Hap#3
(n = 5), and Hap#4 (n = 4), included in two main clades, with Hap#1, Hap#2, and Hap#3
included in clade 1 and Hap#4 included in clade 2 (Figure 2). This clade included only the
sequences from Serra dos Órgãos National Park and Itatiaia National Park, while clade 1
included sequences from all studied sites. Hap#2 was formed exclusively by sequences from
AREI Itapebussus. Seven haplotypes were identified as unique, not forming haplogroups
(Table 1, Figure 2). There were no specific haplogroups formed according to hosts (Figure 2).

4. Discussion
Herein we performed, for the first time, the genetic characterization of pathogenic
leptospires identified in 15 species of small non-flying wild mammals from conservation
units of the Brazilian Atlantic Forest. A high occurrence was found (56%), which agrees
with studies carried out in the same region [21,22]. Another study conducted in small wild
rodents from the southeast Brazilian Atlantic Forest, but in rural areas, revealed a lower
prevalence (21.3%) and host diversity (five species) based on qPCR diagnosis [30]. This is
not surprising, since conservation areas often support greater diversity and abundance of
reservoir hosts, greater environmental persistence of the bacteria, low human impact and
less use of control measures, greater interactions between species and trophic networks, and
less competition with synanthropic species [31]. A study also conducted in conservation
areas of the Brazilian Amazon biome revealed a high prevalence of leptospiral DNA in
small mammals (44.7%) from 16 different species [32], reinforcing that conservation areas,
with their rich biodiversity, can harbor multiple natural reservoirs forLeptospira.
Most of the hosts were from the order Rodentia (n = 83), with emphasis on the genera
Akodon (n = 23) and Mus (n = 21). The genus Akodon, which includes neotropical wild
rodents, has been identified as a major carrier of pathogenic Leptospira in the Atlantic
Forest region of Brazil. Studies have shown that a substantial proportion of Akodon spp.
are PCR-positive for pathogenic Leptospira, highlighting their role as reservoirs in this
environment [21,22]. This suggests that Akodon rodents contribute to the maintenance and
transmission of leptospires in areas where they are prevalent, although their impact may be
more pronounced in rural or forested areas rather than urban settings like Rio de Janeiro.
Studies on Akodon and other sigmodontine rodents in other South American regions, such
as the Paraná Delta in Argentina, further support their involvement in the transmission
of Leptospira. The species Akodon azarae was identified as a host for Leptospira interrogans
serovar Icterohaemorrhagiae, suggesting that these rodents can carry and potentially
transmit zoonotic Leptospira strains across their geographic range, which includes parts
of Brazil [33]. In contrast, the role of Mus musculus in transmitting Leptospira spp. varies
by region. While they can be relevant carriers in certain areas, such as urban settlements
in Nairobi, Kenya [34], and rural settings in Puerto Rico [ 35], their role seems to be less
pronounced in urban areas in Brazil, like in Rio de Janeiro, where Rattus species are the
major reservoirs [36]. Other rodents identified in the present study included Oligoryzomys
nigrips, Trinomys marmosa, Brucepattersonius sp., Delomys altimontanus, Delomys dorsalis,
Oxymycterus sp., and Necromys lasiurus, previously identified as hosts of Leptospira in the
region [21,22,30].
Regarding the marsupials, Didelphis aurita, Monodelphis sp., and Marmosa paraguayana
were herein identified as hosts of L. interrogans. Other studies have investigated marsupials,
particularly opossums, as hosts of Leptospira spp. In a study performed in Southern
Brazil, the white-eared opossum ( Didelphis albiventris) was identified as a reservoir of
pathogenic Leptospira spp. [37]. Another study examined a broader range of wildlife in
Brazil, including opossums, and identified L. santarosai as the prevalent species, with a
higher risk of infection observed in adult and male opossums when compared to their
younger and female counterparts [19]. Additionally, a study conducted in Rio Grande do
Sul, Brazil, detected pathogenic Leptospira spp. DNA in various wild mammals, including
the white-eared opossum. The species L. borgpetersenii and L. interrogans were identified [38].
These studies collectively highlight the significance of marsupials, particularly opossums,
as hosts of Leptospira in Brazil, with potential contributions to the maintenance of the
bacterial transmission cycle.
Regarding the phylogenetic analyses based on the SLST method applied, it was
possible to observe a high genetic identity between the sequences from the present study

Trop. Med. Infect. Dis. 2025, 10, 62 8 of 11
(TN92 = 0.01 ± 0.01; 99% identity) (Figure 2). This can be explained by the geographic
proximity between the studied areas, which present shared environmental features such as
similar climatic and ecological conditions (e.g., temperature, humidity, and water bodies).
Moreover, some Leptospira spp. strains exhibit genetic stability over time, especially if they
are well adapted to their host and/or environment [39], which appears to be the case for
rodent and marsupial hosts in this region of the Atlantic Forest. Limited selective pressure
in certain environments may reduce the rate of genetic divergence [40]. On the other hand,
it is important to note that, while in the Atlantic Forest, a low genetic diversity was observed
among Leptospira spp., a study conducted in the Western Amazon Forest identified three
different species, with high intraspecific genetic variation [32]. This greater genetic diversity
of Leptospira in the Amazon region is probably related to the high biodiversity of hosts
and less fragmentation of the habitat. The Atlantic Forest, with its high fragmentation and
smaller number of reservoir species, may be subject to a genetic bottleneck effect, limiting
the diversity of bacterial lineages [41].
Regarding intraspecific analysis, our results showed the presence of four main hap-
logroups, not related to hosts or geographic locations, except for Hap#2, which was formed
exclusively by sequences from AREI Itapebussus (Figure 2). Importantly, Hap#1 included
the largest number of sequences in the present study (n = 68) that also comprised L. interro-
gans reference sequences from humans, dogs, and urban rats from the Icterohaemorrhagiae
serogroup. It is well known that the clonal subpopulation Fiocruz L1-130 of L. interro-
gans serogroup Icterohaemorrhagiae is widely distributed in Brazil and Latin America
in different hosts with a major zoonotic role [ 42,43]. The data from the present study
demonstrate that small wild mammals from the Atlantic Forest are also reservoirs of this
strain, which seems to be ubiquitarian in that biome. This outcome raises an important
public health concern: L. interrogans from the Icterohaemorrhagiae serogroup is the major
agent of leptospirosis in humans [8], and rodents in forested areas, particularly in regions
like the Atlantic Forest, can act as a direct or indirect link to human infection.
The Atlantic Forest is one of the most biodiverse biomes in the world but is facing
severe degradation due to urbanization, agriculture, and logging, with much of its original
cover already destroyed [44]. It is the most deforested forest in Brazil, and currently, only
12.4% of the original forest remains [ 45]. This degradation has a direct impact on local
ecology and public health, especially on the transmission of zoonotic diseases such as
leptospirosis, which may occur due to different factors: (i) habitat fragmentation and
increased human–wildlife interaction; (ii) disruption of ecosystem balance (disturbed
trophic interactions and bacterial persistence in altered environments); (iii) increased
exposure to contaminated water sources; (iv) changes in biodiversity that may lead to shift
in host species; and (v) climate change, which can promote favorable conditions for the
spread of the bacteria [46].
5. Conclusions
The present study revealed a high genetic identity among pathogenic leptospires
circulating in small non-flying mammals from the southeastern Atlantic Forest biome,
highlighting the presence of a larger haplogroup that includes a highly virulent strain also
detected in humans, dogs, and urban rats (L. interrogans serogroup Icterohaemorrhagiae,
strain Fiocruz L1-130), and evidenced the zoonotic potential of the identified leptospires.
Our results reinforce the role of small mammals, such as rodents and marsupials, as
important carriers of Leptospira interrogans and draw attention to the Atlantic Forest as an
important environment for the circulation and dissemination of the spirochaete. Detecting
virulent strains in animals of different species that inhabit forests and peri-urban areas
warns of the imminent risk to public health, especially in regions where interactions

Trop. Med. Infect. Dis. 2025, 10, 62 9 of 11
between humans and wildlife are frequent. This study highlights the urgent need for
epidemiological surveillance and control actions in southeast Brazil, aiming to mitigate the
transmission of leptospirosis and prevent future outbreaks, especially in highly populated
areas from the Atlantic Forest submitted to intense fragmentation and anthropic actions.
In this context, a One Health approach is fundamental, integrating human, animal, and
environmental health to effectively manage and mitigate the impact of zoonotic diseases
such as leptospirosis.

ARTIGO 4: Distribuição ecológica e associações bioma -hospedeiro de
Leptospira patogênica no Brasil: uma perspectiva de Saúde Única em uma
área tropical
Revista: Acta Tropica (IF= 2.5)

Espécies patogênicas d o gênero Leptospira causam uma zoonose de
distribuição global com ciclos de transmissão complexos envolvendo múltiplos
hospedeiros e ambientes. A vasta diversidade ecológica do Brasil e a alta
circulação de Leptospira spp. exigem abordagens integrativas para compreender
a diversidade genética e a distribuição do patógeno. Compilamos um extenso
conjunto de dados moleculares de Leptospira spp. patogênicas no Brasil,
abrangendo sequências (n=825) de diversos marcadores genéticos e dados de
sequenciamento de genoma completo (WGS) . Um panorama molecular foi
elaborado com base em metadados associados, incluindo espécie hospedeira,
origem geográfica e tipo de fonte (clínica, animal, ambiental). Os registros
abrangem quatro biomas brasileiros, com a maior diversidade e número de
sequências provenientes da Mata Atlântica (69,7%) e da Amazônia (22,2%), com
ênfase em grandes centros urbanos. Leptospira interrogans foi predominante
(74,9%), seguida por L. santarosai (9,8%), L. borgpetersenii (7,2%), L. kirschneri
(3,9%) e L. noguchii (3,9%). Em relação aos sorogrupos, Icterohaemorrhagiae
foi o mais frequente (44,9%). Os hospedeiros incluíram 78 espécies de 12
ordens, entre grandes animais terrestres domésticos (36%), animais terrestres
silvestres (21%), humanos (15%), animais de estim ação (13,8%), roedores
urbanos (7,6%) e mamíferos marinhos (1,3%). Sequências de leptospiras
patogênicas ambientais também foram identificadas (5,3%). Esta análise
molecular integrativa revela a extensa diversidade, amplitude ecológica e
dinâmica complexa de transmissão de leptospiras patogênica nos biomas
Brasileiros. Os resultados reforçam a importância de uma perspectiva de Saúde
Única e fornecem uma base sólida para a vigilância molecular padronizada e
intervenções direcionadas para mitigar a carga da l eptospirose em regiões
tropicais.

Ecological range and host–biome associations of pathogenic Leptospira in
Brazil: A One Health perspective from a tropical area

ABSTRACT
Pathogenic Leptospira spp. cause a globally distributed zoonosis with complex transmission cycles involving
multiple hosts and environments. Brazil’s vast ecological diversity and high Leptospira spp. circulation demand
integrative approaches to understand the pathogen’s genetic diversity and distribution. We compiled an
extensive molecular dataset of pathogenic Leptospira spp. in Brazil, encompassing sequences (n = 825) from
several genetic markers and WGS data. A molecular landscape was provided based on associated metadata,
including host species, geographic origin, and source type (clinical, animal, environmental). Records spanned
four Brazilian biomes, with the highest diversity and number of sequences from the Atlantic Forest (69.7 %) and
Amazon (22.2 %), with emphasis on large urban centers. Leptospira interrogans predominated (74.9 %), followed
by L. santarosai (9.8 %), L. borgpetersenii (7.2 %), L. kirschneri (3.9 %), and L. noguchii (3.9 %). Regarding
serogroups, Icterohaemorrhagiae was the most frequent (44.9 %). Hosts encompassed 78 species from 12 orders,
including domestic large land animals (36 %), wild land animals (21 %), humans (15 %), pets (13.8 %), urban
rodents (7.6 %), and marine mammals (1.3 %). Importantly, sequences from environmental pathogenic lepto-
spires were also identified (5.3 %). This integrative molecular analysis reveals the extensive diversity, ecological
breadth, and complex transmission dynamics of pathogenic Leptospira in those biomes. The findings underscore
the importance of a One Health perspective and provide a robust foundation for standardized molecular sur-
veillance and targeted interventions to mitigate leptospirosis burden in tropical regions.
1. Introduction
Leptospirosis is a widespread zoonotic disease caused by spirochetes
of the genus Leptospira, which includes both free-living and pathogenic
species (Giraud-Gatineau et al., 2024). Traditionally classified by
serology into >300 serovars across over 30 serogroups (Giraud-Gatineau
et al., 2025), Leptospira spp. are also taxonomically divided into 64
species by genomic criteria, grouped into saprophytic (n = 26), inter-
mediate (n = 21), and pathogenic (n = 17) clades (Vincent et al., 2019).
The disconnect between serological and molecular classification systems
underscores the need for integrative approaches in epidemiological
surveillance.
Pathogenic Leptospira infect a wide range of vertebrate hosts, with
over 160 mammal species identified as reservoirs or incidental hosts
(Cilia et al., 2020, 2021). The bacteria are mainly excreted in urine and
disseminated through contaminated water and soil. Reservoir hosts,
such as rodents and livestock, can excrete viable bacteria for extended
periods, maintaining environmental contamination and enabling
transmission to incidental hosts, including humans (Putz and Nally,
2020). Transmission dynamics are influenced by ecological factors such
as flooding, soil characteristics, and reservoir host abundance (Soni
et al., 2024), highlighting the intrinsic links among human, animal, and
environmental health that underpin the One Health framework. This
integrative perspective is crucial for understanding how ecological,
climatic, and social drivers collectively shape the emergence and
persistence of leptospirosis (Antoniolli et al., 2024).
Human leptospirosis remains a significant global health concern,
with the highest incidence in tropical and subtropical regions, but also
reported in temperate areas, often following animal outbreaks (Cataldo
et al., 2024). Annually, an estimated one million cases and 60,000
deaths occur worldwide (Costa et al., 2015). Among tropical countries,
Brazil stands out as a major hotspot for transmission due to its vast
geographical extension, ecological heterogeneity, and intense human-
–animal–environment interactions (Sohn-Hausner et al., 2023).

Leptospirosis is endemic and often reaches epidemic proportions during
the rainy season, particularly in urban centers with poor sanitation and
high rodent infestation (Galan et al., 2021). An average of 3600 cases
and 375 deaths are reported, with Southeast and South regions
concentrating the highest case burdens (Linhares et al., 2024).
Clinical presentation ranges from mild, self-limiting febrile illness to
severe forms such as Weil’s disease and severe pulmonary hemorrhagic
syndrome, with about 10 % of patients developing life-threatening
complications (Nicodemo and Duarte-Neto, 2021). Diagnosis is often
hampered by symptom overlap with other febrile illnesses and by
limited access to confirmatory laboratory tests such as the microscopic
agglutination test (MAT), contributing to underreporting (Ciurariu
et al., 2025; Esteves et al., 2025). Prevention includes rodent control,
avoidance of potentially contaminated water, personal protective
equipment, and, where available, vaccination, although current human
vaccines offer short-lived, serovar-specific immunity and are limited to a
few countries (Barazzone et al., 2021; de Oliveira et al., 2022; Sykes
et al., 2022a).
In animals, leptospirosis is widespread, affecting species from do-
mestic livestock to wildlife. Dogs commonly develop acute hepatorenal
disease (Costa et al., 2022a), while cattle frequently present with
chronic reproductive disorders such as Bovine Genital Leptospirosis, a
silent economically significant syndrome (Loureiro and Lilenbaum,
2020). Rodents and other small mammals often act as asymptomatic
carriers, maintaining environmental contamination (Mohd-Taib et al.,
2020). Control in animals requires an integrated approach combining
antibiotic therapy, vaccination, and environmental management, with
varying efficacy depending on host species, infecting serogroup, and
epidemiological context (Martins and Lilenbaum, 2015; Soo et al.,
2020). Environmental persistence of the pathogen and the diversity of
animal reservoirs make eradication unlikely, underscoring the impor-
tance of One Health strategies to reduce transmission at the
human-animal-environment interface (Naing et al., 2019). In Brazil, this
challenge is magnified by the country’s exceptional ecological diversity,
encompassing six major biomes (Amazon, Atlantic Forest, Cerrado,
Caatinga, Pantanal, and Pampa), each harboring distinct climates,
wildlife communities, and degrees of anthropogenic pressure (IBGE,
2019). Such environmental heterogeneity creates unique
eco-epidemiological scenarios for Leptospira maintenance, adaptation,
and transmission.
Although routine surveillance in developing countries still relies
heavily on serological data (Nardoni Marteli et al., 2022), molecular
tools have become essential for species-level identification, outbreak
investigation, and tracing of transmission routes. Markers such as 16S
rRNA, secY, lipL32, and multilocus sequence typing (MLST) schemes,
along with whole-genome sequencing (WGS), have provided taxonomic
identification and enabled comparative analyses of circulating strains
(Di Azevedo and Lilenbaum, 2021; Sykes et al., 2022b). The increasing
availability of these genetic data from public repositories enables
large-scale in silico studies that integrate genetic, geographic, and
ecological information. Despite the availability of hundreds of Leptospira
sequences from Brazilian isolates and clinical samples, most previous
studies have focused on specific hosts, regions, or outbreaks, resulting in
fragmented knowledge of the pathogen’s molecular diversity and
ecological distribution. There is still a lack of nationwide integrative
analyses that combine data from multiple hosts, ecosystems, and biomes
under a unified molecular and ecological perspective. An integrative
approach that bridges data across hosts and biomes is therefore crucial
to understand transmission patterns in such a complex tropical land-
scape. By compiling and analyzing genetic data from humans, domestic
animals, wildlife, and environmental sources across all major Brazilian
biomes, this study bridges that gap and provides the first comprehensive
molecular overview of pathogenic Leptospira in Brazil, advancing the
understanding of transmission dynamics and host–environment con-
nectivity within a One Health framework in a tropical context.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Data collection and curation
A comprehensive database was compiled to assess the genetic di-
versity and circulation patterns of pathogenic Leptospira species in
Brazil, including human, animal, and environmental records. Nucleotide
sequences were retrieved from the NCBI GenBank database using the
search string “Leptospira AND Brazil” last accessed on 15 July 2025
(GenBank release 257.0). The search covered all available records
deposited between 2009 and 2025. Only sequences corresponding to
genetically characterized isolates, with an identified Leptospira species
and associated metadata including host/source and geographical loca-
tion, were included. Sequences labeled only as “Leptospira sp.” were
excluded because they lack reliable species-level identification, which is
essential for accurate phylogenetic and epidemiological inferences

(Riley, 2018). Although some of these records may contain partial
metadata, their exclusion minimizes potential misclassification and
ensures consistency in downstream analyses. We acknowledge that this
criterion may slightly reduce the representation of poorly characterized
or newly described taxa, but it strengthens the reliability of species-level
comparisons across datasets. Only pathogenic species were included,
specifically, members of the P1 clade as defined by Vincent et al. (2019).
Intermediate and saprophytic species were excluded.
Each eligible record was manually reviewed and annotated with the
following attributes: GenBank accession number, Leptospira species,
strain or sample identification (ID), genetic marker applied, serovar/
serogroup (when available), host species (taxonomic and ecological
categories) or environmental source, geographical location (city,
geographic region, and biome), and associated reference. Metadata
referring to host identity, sampling location, and serovar information
were cross-checked with the original publications cited in GenBank
whenever available, to ensure accuracy and consistency. Records with
incomplete, ambiguous, or conflicting metadata were retained only if
the core attributes (species, genetic marker, and host or source) could be
confidently verified; otherwise, they were excluded from the dataset.
The data was organized in an Excel spreadsheet.
2.2. Host and geographical categorization
To enable ecological and epidemiological comparisons, besides
taxonomic categorization of host species, they were classified into seven
broad categories: "Domestic large land animal", "Wild land animal",
"Pet", "Human", "Marine mammal", "Urban rodent", and "Environment".
These categories were based on ecological and epidemiological criteria
widely used in zoonotic surveillance frameworks (e.g., OIE and CDC
guidelines) but were adapted to reflect the host diversity represented in
the dataset. Similarly, geographical locations were also assigned to one
of the five major Brazilian biomes, defined according to the Brazilian
Institute of Geography and Statistics (IBGE): "Amazon", "Atlantic Forest",
"Pampa", "Cerrado", and "Caatinga", based on the original collection site.
The Atlantic Ocean was also included as a separate category (coastal-
marine system – CMS).
The Amazon is a humid rainforest with >2000 mm annual rainfall
and exceptional biodiversity (Flores et al., 2024). The Atlantic Forest
along the eastern coast is highly fragmented and rich in endemic species
(Colombo and Joly, 2010). The Caatinga is a semi-arid region with
xerophytic vegetation and seasonal droughts (da Silva and Lacher,
2020). The Cerrado, a tropical savanna, exhibits a grassland–woodland
mosaic and marked dry season (Colli et al., 2020). The Pampa, in
southern Brazil, consists of temperate grasslands (Roesch et al., 2009),
while the Pantanal is a vast wetland with seasonal flooding (Wantzen
et al., 2024). The CMS includes estuaries, mangroves, and oceanic wa-
ters linking terrestrial and marine ecosystems (´Alvares-Da-Silva et al.,
2022).. Fig. 1 shows the geographical divisions of Brazil and its biomes.
2.3. Data analysis and host-species inventory
Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the number and pro-
portion of Leptospira species, serogroups, host categories, and biomes
represented in the dataset. The data compiled in spreadsheets were
analyzed using the R programming environment (version 4.5.1; R Core
Team, 2024). The dataset was imported using the readxl package.
The final table, including absolute counts and percentages, was exported
using the writexl package for further tabular presentation. No infer-
ential or quantitative statistical analyses (e.g., species richness or di-
versity indices) were performed, as the study was designed to provide a
descriptive and integrative overview of molecular records rather than to
test specific hypotheses.
Additionally, a host-species inventory table was manually created to
document all known hosts of pathogenic Leptospira in Brazil based on
genetically confirmed records. This matrix included the taxonomic
classes, orders, and species (both scientific and common names), the
Leptospira species detected in each host, and the biome(s) where these
interactions were recorded. Scientific names of host species were vali-
dated using the NCBI Taxonomy Browser (available at: https://www.
ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/taxonomy).

2.4. Geospatial mapping of pathogenic Leptospira occurrence data in
Brazil
To visualize the spatial distribution of genetically characterized
pathogenic Leptospira species in Brazil, we generated thematic maps
using Python 3.12 (https://www.python.org/) in a WSL (Windows
Subsystem for Linux) environment. The analysis was performed using
the following core packages: pandas (https://pandas.pydata.org/) for
data manipulation, geopandas (https://geopandas.org/) for spatial
operations and shapefile handling, shapely (https://shapely.readth
edocs.io/) for geometric construction of point data, and matplotlib
(https://matplotlib.org/) for map visualization and figure export.
A curated spreadsheet was compiled, containing three columns: (1)
Leptospira species name, (2) latitude, and (3) longitude of the munici-
pality where the species was identified. All entries corresponded to
genetically confirmed isolates, and geographic coordinates were
manually cross-referenced and standardized based on official IBGE data
( https://www.ibge.gov.br/). When precise coordinates were not pro-
vided, the centroid of the corresponding municipality or state was used
as a proxy.
Two types of maps were constructed: one overlaid on the political
boundaries of Brazilian states, allowing for interpretation in terms of
public health jurisdictions, and another overlaid on biome regions, to
emphasize the environmental and ecological distribution patterns of the
species. For the first map, we used the official shapefile of Brazilian
federative units, including CMS, downloaded from the official IBGE
geographic data server (FTP repository) (Available at https://ftp.ibge.
gov.br/).
The second visualization was generated using the official shapefile of
Brazilian biomes and CMS, also obtained from IBGE. All geospatial data,
including the shapefiles of Brazilian states and biomes, were
standardized to the WGS84 geographic coordinate reference system
(EPSG:4326). It expresses locations in decimal degrees of latitude and
longitude and ensures compatibility across datasets. In both maps, each
pathogenic Leptospira species was assigned a unique color, and the size
of the circles was scaled proportionally to the number of occurrences
using a multiplicative factor (count × 60) to enhance visual discrimi-
nation. To ensure visual consistency, the same circle scaling factor was
applied across both maps. As the data were obtained by convenience
sampling, the aim of this visualization was not to infer prevalence or
abundance, but rather to highlight the ecological range and known
distribution of pathogenic Leptospira in Brazil, based on genetically
validated records.
3. Results
3.1. Dataset composition and overview of pathogenic Leptospira
circulation
A total of 825 genetically characterized sequences of pathogenic
Leptospira were included in the final dataset, including those from the
genes secY (n = 546; 66.2 %), 16S rRNA (n = 120; 14.6 %), lipL32 (n =
38; 4.6 %), gyrB (n = 4; 0.5 %), and pfkB (n = 1; 0.1 %) (Table 1).
Additionally, data from MLST (n = 17; 2 %) schemes and WGS (n = 99,
12 %) were also included. Each record was linked to a specific host or
environmental source and a defined geographical location within Brazil.
Detailed information is provided in Supplementary Material 1, and
general statistical data are shown in Table 1.
The sequences comprised 7 formally identified species, including L.
interrogans (n = 618/ 74.9 %), L. santarosai (n = 81; 9.8 %), L. borgpe-
tersenii (n = 59; 7.2 %), L. noguchii (n = 32; 3.9 %), L. kirschneri (n = 32;
3.9 %), L. yasudae (n = 2; 0.2 %), and L. stimsonii (n = 1; 0.1 %).

Regarding serogrouping, only 312/ 825 (37.8 %) of deposits had a
defined serovar and/or serogroup. From these, Icterohaemorrhagiae
was the most frequent serogroup (n = 140; 44.9 %), followed by Sejroe
(n = 95; 30.5 %), Pomona (n = 17/ 5.5 %), Grippotyphosa (n = 14; 4.6
%), and Autumnalis (n = 12; 3.8 %). Other serogroups were identified,
but in a few isolates (Table 1; Supplementary Material 1).
Regarding host/source, the majority of sequences were from do-
mestic large land animals (n = 297; 36 %), followed by wild land ani-
mals (n = 173; 21 %) and humans (n = 125; 15 %). Pets (cats and dogs)
were identified in 114 deposits (13.8 %), while urban rodents and ma-
rine mammals were hosts from 64 (7.6 %) and 11 (1.3 %) of pathogenic
Leptospira, respectively. Samples from environmental sources, like
puddle, sewage, and soil, totaled 44 records (5.3 %) (Table 1; Supple-
mentary Material 1).
The Atlantic Forest was the biome with the largest number of path-
ogenic Leptospira records (n = 575; 69.7 %), with emphasis on large
urban centers, such as Salvador, Rio de Janeiro, and S˜ao Paulo, located
in the Northeast and Southeast regions, which had the highest number of
records (44.7 % and 25.6 %, respectively). The regions North and South
of the country totaled 183 (22.2 %) and 62 records (7.5 %), respectively.
Amazon, Pampa, and Cerrado totaled 183 (22.2 %), 48 (5.8 %), and 8 (1
%) occurrences, respectively. Eleven marine mammals were identified
as hosts on the Southern Brazilian coast. No records were found in the
Central-West region, and in the Pantanal and Caatinga biomes. In terms
of landscape, most records originated from the rural (n = 303; 36.7 %)
and urban (n = 287; 34.8 %) areas, followed by sylvatic (n = 140; 17 %)
and peri‑urban (n = 95; 11.5 %) environments (Table 1; Supplementary
Material 1). Overall, the integrated dataset reveals that L. interrogans
was predominantly detected in urban environments, whereas L. borg-
petersenii, L. kirschneri, and L. noguchii were more frequently reported in
rural areas. Leptospira santarosai showed a more balanced distribution,
occurring predominantly in rural and peri‑urban settings. No records of
L. noguchii were found in peri‑urban environments, and L. kirschneri was
not detected in sylvatic areas.
3.2. Host range of Leptospira species
In total, the data encompassed isolates/samples from 78 vertebrate
host species, including terrestrial, arboreal, aquatic, and synanthropic
mammals, as well as a few reptile species. The majority of detections
occurred in mammals, encompassing nine different taxonomic orders,
including both domestic and wild species. Arctiodactyls, rodents, car-
nivores, and primates were the most common hosts (Table 1, Table 2,
Supplementary Material 1).
Among all hosts, Bos taurus (domestic cattle) exhibited the highest
Leptospira species richness, harboring five different species: L. inter-
rogans, L. noguchii, L. kirschneri, L. borgpetersenii, and L. santarosai. Other
hosts with high species diversity included domestic dogs (Canis lupus
familiaris), associated with four species, and capybaras (Hydrochoerus
hydrochaeris), with three species (Table 2, Supplementary Material 1).
Several wild mammals were found to carry multiple Leptospira spe-
cies. Notably, marsupials of the genera Didelphis, Marmosa, and Mono-
delphis, as well as various small rodents such as Akodon, Delomys,
Oligoryzomys, and Proechimys, were recurrent hosts, primarily associated
with L. interrogans and L. santarosai. Additionally, a notable number of
host–pathogen associations involved bat species, which represented a
taxonomically and ecologically diverse group within the dataset. At least
14 bat species from multiple genera, such as Artibeus, Carollia, Glosso-
phaga, Molossus, Myotis, Desmodus, and Tadarida, were found infected
with Leptospira, predominantly L. interrogans. These species included
frugivorous, nectarivorous, and hematophagous bats (Table 2, Supple-
mentary Material 1).
In addition to terrestrial mammals, some marine mammals, such as
the Franciscana dolphin (Pontoporia blainvillei) and fur seals (Arctoce-
phalus spp.), were also found infected with L. interrogans. Other occa-
sional detections in non-mammalian hosts included reptiles like the boa,
tegu lizard, and caiman (Table 2, Supplementary material 1).
3.3. Geographic distribution of Leptospira species
Pathogenic Leptospira species have been genetically reported in 11
states, including four Brazilian biomes and the coastal marine environ-
ments, with marked variation in both species’ richness and spatial dis-
tribution. In addition to the five species previously reported in the hosts,
L. yasudae and L. stimsonii have been reported from environmental
sources in Bahia and Rio de Janeiro, respectively, both in the Atlantic
Forest. Overall, L. interrogans was the most widely distributed species,
present in all biomes and across the largest number of states. Other
species exhibited more localized patterns, typically restricted to fewer
regions (Fig. 2).
The highest concentration of records was observed in the South-
eastern and Southern regions of the country, particularly in the states of
S˜ao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, and Rio Grande do Sul. These areas exhibited
not only the largest number of records but also the highest diversity of
Leptospira species per location. A high number of L. interrogans occur-
rences was also recorded in the Northeastern state of Bahia, notably
around the city of Salvador. In contrast, central regions of the country
showed none or fewer records, and the northern region presented more
scattered detections (Fig. 2A).
Regarding the biomes, the Atlantic Forest harbored the greatest
number of occurrences, with records of all major Leptospira species. The
Amazon biome also presented a high frequency of detections, particu-
larly of L. interrogans, L. borgpetersenii, and L. santarosai. The Pampa
biome showed a remarkable diversity of Leptospira species, despite its
lower representation compared to the Atlantic Forest and Amazon. The
Cerrado had only a few records, while the Pantanal and Caatinga
showed no data so far. In addition, several occurrences were located in
the marine domain, along the Atlantic Ocean coast, particularly
involving L. interrogans in marine mammals (Fig. 2B).
Overall, the dataset revealed clear ecological and spatial patterns in
the distribution of pathogenic Leptospira across Brazil. Leptospira inter-
rogans predominated at urban and peri‑urban interfaces, particularly in
synanthropic and domestic hosts, reflecting its adaptation to anthrop-
ized environments and rodent-associated cycles. In contrast, L. santar-
osai, L. noguchii, and L. kirschneri were more frequent in rural and
wildlife contexts, spanning diverse biomes and host groups. Cattle and
dogs emerged as major multi-host bridges, connecting urban, rural, and
sylvatic transmission networks.
4. Discussion
4.1. Overview of species, hosts, and ecological contexts of Leptospira in
Brazil
Based on an extensive survey and analysis of genetic and ecological
data of Leptospira spp. in Brazil, this study compiled the most compre-
hensive molecular datasets of this pathogen in Brazil to date, encom-
passing 825 sequences from multiple genetic targets, including secY,
16S rRNA, lipL32, rpoB, MLST loci, and whole genome sequences
(Table 1, Supplementary Material 1). The sequences were deposited
between 2009 and 2025, reflecting the progressive adoption of molec-
ular tools for leptospirosis surveillance in Brazil in the last decades. The
inclusion of diverse markers allowed for broader taxonomic represen-
tation and geographic coverage across hosts and environments. This
approach reflects both the historical progression of molecular di-
agnostics in leptospirosis and the growing availability of sequence data
from various surveillance and research efforts. On the other hand, this
multi-locus dataset highlights an important gap in standardization,
which underscores the need for coordinated surveillance and research
frameworks adopting molecular targets with both taxonomic and
epidemiological relevance, as previously proposed (Di Azevedo and
Lilenbaum, 2021). Noteworthy that the data analyzed in this study do
