not reflect the actual prevalence of Leptospira infection in Brazil, as only
records with available species-level genetic sequences were included.
Numerous studies based on serological assays or non-sequenced mo-
lecular detections were excluded, suggesting that the true geographic
and host distribution of pathogenic Leptospira in the country is likely
much broader than depicted here. Additionally, the dataset exhibits
sampling biases inherent to the available molecular records, with a
predominance of secY sequences and isolates from the Atlantic Forest
region. This uneven representation likely reflects methodological pref-
erences and the concentration of molecular research infrastructure in
southeastern Brazil. Such heterogeneity may influence perceived pat-
terns of genetic diversity and should be considered when interpreting
ecological and phylogenetic trends.
Despite the known diversity of pathogenic Leptospira species
(Vincent et al., 2019), the predominance of L. interrogans (74.9 %)
(Table 1) mirrors its global importance as the most frequent agent of
animal and human disease (Rajapakse et al., 2025). In Brazil, it is the
most widespread species, including wild, rural and urban scenarios (da
Cunha et al., 2016; de Albuquerque et al., 2017a; Jorge et al., 2018; Paz
et al., 2019; Rodamilans et al., 2020; Siqueira et al., 2020; Ulsenheimer
et al., 2022; Gomes et al., 2022; Freitas et al., 2024;Di Azevedo et al.,
2025). Other species, such as L. santarosai, L. borgpetersenii, L. noguchii,
and L. kirschneri, were also present, although at lower frequencies (3–10
%), suggesting underreporting or reduced molecular surveillance in the
hosts or regions where they may circulate more prominently.
Leptospira santarosai has been recognized as an important circulating
species in the Americas (Chinchilla et al., 2023). It has been implicated
in reproductive disorders in livestock (Di Azevedo et al., 2021; Aym´ee
et al., 2022a), zoonotic transmission in tropical settings (Pel´aez Sanchez
et al., 2016), as well as asymptomatic infections in dogs (Miotto et al.,
2016) and wild animals (Moreno et al., 2016; Medeiros et al., 2020;
Vieira et al., 2019).
Notably, the vast majority of L. borgpetersenii hosts are cattle, and the
species has been considered an important agent of bovine genital
leptospirosis (Aym´ee et al., 2024). Evidence of vertical transmission in
cattle highlights its complex transmission pathways, which are strongly
influenced by host density rather than environmental factors (Bulach
et al., 2006). Infections in urban rodents, wild animals, and dogs have
also been reported for this species (Moreno et al., 2016; Vieira et al.,
2019; Ulsenheimer et al., 2024, 2025).
An outbreak in goats involving reproductive disorders has been
associated with L. noguchii infection (Aym´ee et al., 2022b), and the
species has also been reported in dogs, cows, and small mammals
(Guedes et al., 2021; Loureiro et al., 2020; Medeiros et al., 2020; San-
t’Anna et al., 2021). Leptospira kirschneri was associated with a human
leptospirosis case in southern Brazil, caused by a strain genetically
related to a canine isolate from the same region (da Cunha et al., 2016).
Other hosts include horses, bovines, and capybaras (Hamond et al.,
2016; Jaeger et al., 2019; Guedes et al., 2021). Interestingly, the
occurrence of the recently described environmental pathogenic species
L. yasudae and L. stimsonii (Casanovas-Massana et al., 2020), although
rare (n = 3), reinforces the potential for overlooked diversity within the
genus and supports recent taxonomic updates derived from genomic
analyses. Similarly, studies conducted in the Amazon region have
genetically identified potentially new Leptospira species circulating in
bats and cattle, although further studies are necessary for their formal
description and validation (Guedes et al., 2019; Di Azevedo et al., 2023;
Verde et al., 2024).
Regarding serogroup information, <40 % of the sequences were
linked to a defined serovar and/or serogroup (Supplementary Table 1).
This low proportion reflects not a failure in the deposit process or
metadata curation, but rather a methodological limitation related to the
need for viable bacterial isolates to perform the Microscopic Aggluti-
nation Test (MAT), the current standard for serogroup identification.
Since Leptospira spp. are notoriously fastidious and slow-growing or-
ganisms, bacterial culturing remains a major bottleneck in routine
diagnostics and surveillance. Moreover, the MAT requires a well-
equipped laboratory, skilled personnel, and access to a panel of live
reference cultures, which are often unavailable in low-resource settings
(Ciurariu et al., 2025). These constraints limit the widespread applica-
tion of serological classification, especially in remote or resource-limited
regions. Among the classified records, the predominance of the
serogroup Icterohaemorrhagiae (Table 1) is consistent with its
well-documented global and national distribution, being the most
commonly reported serogroup in both human and canine acute lepto-
spirosis cases (Hagedoorn et al., 2024). As a rodent-adapted serogroup,
its high detection rates are typically linked to urban transmission cycles
maintained by R. norvegicus. However, the occurrence of serogroup
Icterohaemorrhagiae detected in the genital tract of cattle and horses
represents an unexpected finding, raising important questions about its
potential role in genital leptospirosis and sexual transmission, and
revealing an underexplored epidemiological interface. Several hypoth-
eses could explain this observation, including cross-species adaptation
or spillover from rodent reservoirs, host–pathogen coevolution leading
to niche expansion, or even diagnostic artifacts resulting from serolog-
ical cross-reactivity or environmental contamination. Regardless of the
underlying mechanism, this finding underscores the need for targeted
molecular and experimental studies to confirm tissue tropism, assess
reproductive transmission potential, and elucidate the evolutionary
dynamics of Icterohaemorrhagiae in non-traditional hosts. Notably, this
contrasts with the expected host–serogroup associations, as Icter-
ohaemorrhagiae is typically linked to acute infections and urban
transmission, whereas the predominance of Sejroe-related records re-
mains consistent with its recognized role in livestock infections,
particularly in cattle, and its known involvement in chronic, reproduc-
tive forms of leptospirosis (Loureiro and Lilenbaum, 2020).
The spatial patterns observed highlight the ecological differentiation
among Leptospira species. The predominance of L. interrogans in urban
environments supports its adaptation to synanthropic cycles involving
rodents and domestic animals, commonly associated with human
infection risk in densely populated areas (Bradley and Lockaby, 2023).
In contrast, the higher occurrence of L. borgpetersenii, L. kirschneri, and L.
noguchii in rural landscapes reflects their maintenance in livestock and
wildlife hosts, consistent with previous reports of host-associated
transmission in agricultural settings (Guedes et al., 2019; Soares et al.,
2020). The intermediate distribution of L. santarosai across rural and
peri‑urban areas suggests ecological flexibility and potential overlap
between domestic and sylvatic transmission networks (Chinchilla et al.,
2023). Together, these findings underscore how landscape heterogene-
ity influences Leptospira circulation and host connectivity across Brazil.
However, they should be interpreted cautiously, as the dataset results
from opportunistic submissions and unequal research efforts across re-
gions and host groups.
4.2. Host range and ecological roles in Leptospira transmission
The host distribution in the dataset demonstrates the wide host range
of pathogenic Leptospira in Brazil, with sequences retrieved from a
diverse array of domestic animals (cattle, pigs, goats, sheep, and horses),
wildlife (small mammals, bats, large carnivores), pets (dogs and cats),
and humans (Table 1). From a taxonomic point of view, 78 host species
were identified, including two classes (mammals and reptiles) from 12
distinct orders (Tables 1 and 2). Of these, the most notable were Artio-
dactyla (ungulate mammals, like ruminants and pigs), Rodentia (ro-
dents), Carnivora (mainly dogs), and Primates (humans) (Tables 1 and
2). This diversity reinforces the classical concept of leptospirosis as a
multi-host zoonosis, in which transmission cycles are maintained by a
wide variety of species with differing epidemiological roles (Belsare
et al., 2022). Similar host diversity has also been reported in studies
from other endemic regions, underscoring the global relevance of this
ecological plasticity (Dietrich et al., 2018; Ferreira et al., 2020; Motto
et al., 2021; Sluydts et al., 2022; Wainaina et al., 2024). From a One

Health perspective, the observed host spectrum reveals potential
maintenance and spillover dynamics among different ecological com-
partments. Cattle and other domestic livestock, along with synanthropic
and wild rodents, likely act as primary maintenance reservoirs, sus-
taining endemic transmission (Martins and Lilenbaum, 2015).
Conversely, dogs and humans are more often incidental hosts, reflecting
spillover events facilitated by shared environments, water sources, or
contaminated soil (Bierque et al., 2020).
Among the host species identified with genetically confirmed Lep-
tospira infection in Brazil, a subset appears to represent exclusive or
nearly exclusive records for the country, with no equivalent molecular
documentation elsewhere. These include forest-dwelling small mam-
mals such as Brucepattersonius spp., Delomys spp., Akodon cursor, Akodon
montensis, Monodelphis glirina and Trinomys spp., most of which are
endemic to Brazilian biomes (https://www.gbif.org) and rarely included
in global leptospirosis surveys. This high number of host species exclu-
sively reported in Brazil highlights the country’s pivotal role in
expanding the global understanding of Leptospira ecology, especially in
wildlife. Noteworthy, Brazil’s exceptionally rich biodiversity and
ecological heterogeneity support a broader range of potential reservoir
hosts than is typically encountered in temperate or more homogenized
environments. These findings reinforce the idea that forest-dwelling
small mammals serve as important enzootic reservoirs in sylvatic
transmission cycles, a pattern also seen in parts of South and Central
America (Benavidez et al., 2019; Souza Rocha et al., 2020; Silva-Ramos
et al., 2025), but less documented in temperate zones. Conversely, many
hosts identified in this study, such as cattle, dogs, rats, and horses, have
also been reported as leptospiral carriers in other tropical areas,
evidencing extensive evidence of their roles as reservoirs beyond Brazil
(Orjuela et al., 2022; Andrade-Silveira et al., 2024).
The predominance of sequences from domestic large land animals,
particularly livestock such as cattle and pigs, reflects their epidemio-
logical relevance as key reservoirs of pathogenic Leptospira. This finding
aligns with previous studies indicating high infection rates and chronic
carriage in these species ( Fernandes et al., 2020; Guedes et al., 2021;
Gomes et al., 2022), which not only sustain transmission cycles within
animal populations but also pose a direct zoonotic threat to humans
through occupational and environmental exposure (Alinaitwe et al.,
2019). The substantial proportion of sequences from wild animals
highlights the importance of wildlife in maintaining leptospiral diversity
and facilitating spillover events, especially in ecotones or areas of
habitat fragmentation (Helman et al., 2023; Verde et al., 2024).
Conversely, the low number of human-derived sequences likely reflects
limited molecular surveillance and underestimates the true burden,
given the diversity of animal reservoirs and environmental conditions
that favor Leptospira transmission in Brazil (Browne et al., 2022).

Likewise, urban rodents represented only 7.6 % of the records, which is
inconsistent with their recognized role as key reservoirs in urban
leptospirosis cycles (Soni et al., 2024). This underrepresentation likely
stems from sampling and reporting biases, as molecular data on rodents
are often scarce, localized, or not publicly deposited. It underscores the
need for expanded genomic surveillance of rodent populations, espe-
cially in urban settings.
Importantly, 114 records (13.8 %) were associated with dogs,
underscoring their growing recognition as key players in the epidemi-
ology of leptospirosis. Recent studies have highlighted the role of dogs
not only as incidental hosts, but also as potential maintenance hosts in
urban and peri‑urban areas, where they may act as a bridge between
rodents, humans, and other domestic animals (Sant’anna et al., 2017;
Santos et al., 2021; Paz et al., 2025). The relevance of canine leptospi-
rosis has been further supported by national seroprevalence studies,
which report consistent exposure to serogroups commonly associated
with disease in humans and dogs, particularly Icterohaemorrhagiae,
even in asymptomatic animals (Pinheiro et al., 2022; Ricardo et al.,
2024).
Notably, the dataset also revealed host–pathogen associations in
bats, with at least 14 species found infected. These included frugivorous
(Artibeus, Carollia), nectarivorous (Glossophaga), insectivorous (Tadar-
ida, Molossus, Myotis), and hematophagous (Desmodus) taxa. The pre-
dominance of L. interrogans suggests widespread exposure in this group,
regardless of feeding habits. On the other hand, a high diversity of
Leptospira species was found in bats from Colombia, in the Magdalena-
Caribbean tropical humid zonobiome (Monroy et al., 2021). Recent
studies in Brazil have highlighted bats as emerging reservoirs of Lep-
tospira, particularly in the periurban and forest-edge environments, with
high infection rates in Amazonian and Atlantic Forest regions (Di Aze-
vedo et al., 2023; Verde et al., 2024). Their mobility and capacity to
occupy both natural and anthropized habitats make them epidemio-
logically relevant for spillover and dispersal events, especially in light of
global concerns around bat-borne zoonoses.
Although not an exclusive species of Brazil, records of active infec-
tion in capybaras by Multiple species of Leptospira are, to date, docu-
mented mainly in Brazil. These largest living rodents are highly adapted
to semi-aquatic environments, emerging as an epidemiologically sig-
nificant host in the country (da Silva et al., 2023; Ulsenheimer et al.,
2024). In this study, they were found carrying four distinct Leptospira
species (L. interrogans, L. kirschneri, L. borgpetersenii, and L. santarosai)
across multiple biomes, reinforcing their role in both sylvatic and syn-
anthropic transmission cycles. Their gregarious behavior, frequent use
of shared water bodies, and increasing presence in urban, periurban, and
agricultural landscapes facilitate environmental contamination and
cross-species transmission, particularly with livestock and humans.
Unlike similar rodents in other regions, capybaras demonstrate a
consistent association with leptospiral shedding, and may act as
amplifier hosts, sustaining high bacterial loads and contributing to the
environmental persistence of the pathogen (de Albuquerque et al.,
2017b).
The identification of Leptospira in marine mammals (n = 11) high-
lights an emerging and understudied component of the epidemiological
cycle, particularly in coastal and estuarine ecosystems. These findings
align with growing evidence that aquatic mammals, including pinni-
peds, cetaceans, and manatees, can be exposed to and infected by
pathogenic Leptospira, likely through contact with contaminated fresh-
water runoff, sewage discharge, or infected prey (Torres et al., 2025). In
this context, marine mammals may serve not only as incidental hosts but
also as effective sentinels of environmental contamination and
ecosystem health. Their infections can signal broader ecological risks,
including the potential spillover to humans and domestic animals in
coastal communities where human–wildlife–environment interfaces are
intensifying.
Taken together, these patterns highlight distinct functional roles
among host groups in Leptospira transmission networks. Livestock
species such as cattle and pigs primarily sustain enzootic cycles in rural
environments, while synanthropic and companion animals, particularly
dogs and rodents, act as bridge hosts facilitating pathogen spillover to
humans. Recognizing these transmission interfaces is essential for
prioritizing control and surveillance strategies under the One Health
framework.

circulation
The spatial analysis revealed marked heterogeneity in the distribu-
tion of pathogenic Leptospira species across Brazil, highlighting both
regional hotspots and ecological gradients (Table 1, Table 2, Fig. 2).

While L. interrogans demonstrated a broad geographic range , detected in
all major biomes and landscapes, coastal environments, and across 11
states , other species exhibited more localized distributions, suggesting
ecological or surveillance-related constraints. The Southeast and South
regions, particularly the states of S˜ao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, and Rio
Grande do Sul, presented the highest number of records and the greatest
species richness per location, mainly in urban and rural areas (Table 1,
Fig. 2A). It likely reflects a combination of factors, including greater
research infrastructure, historical investment in surveillance, urban
population density, and environmental conditions conducive to trans-
mission, such as frequent flooding and rodent infestation (Nardoni
Marteli et al., 2022; Michelon et al., 2025). These regions are also sites of
major zoonotic outbreaks, often linked to L. interrogans serogroup
Icterohaemorrhagiae, particularly in urban areas with inadequate san-
itary conditions (Costa et al., 2022b; Teles et al., 2023; Linhares et al.,
2024). Interestingly, Salvador, in the Northeast region, also showed a
high number of L. interrogans detections. This corroborates epidemio-
logical data indicating recurrent outbreaks in this region and suggests
that Leptospira transmission is not confined to southern urban centers,
but also affects tropical coastal cities, where socioenvironmental vul-
nerabilities persist (Nabity et al., 2020; Khalil et al., 2021; de Oliveira
et al., 2024).
From an ecological perspective, the Atlantic Forest biome stood out
as a major hotspot, with occurrences of all major pathogenic species,
including the rarely reported L. yasudae and L. stimsonii (Fig. 2B). The
high diversity in this biome likely results from its complex mosaic of
urban, rural, and forested environments, enabling overlapping trans-
mission cycles among domestic animals, wildlife, and humans (Martins
and Lilenbaum, 2015). Likewise, the Amazon biome also harbored a
high frequency of Leptospira species, particularly L. interrogans, L. san-
tarosai, and L. borgpetersenii, reflecting both its biodiversity and the
growing body of studies focused on sylvatic hosts in the region (Guedes
et al., 2019; Medeiros et al., 2020; de Souza Rocha et al., 2022; Gomes
et al., 2022; Di Azevedo et al., 2023; Verde et al., 2024). Of note, the
Pampa biome, despite a lower number of records, showed a considerable
species diversity. This may reflect unique ecological dynamics in
southern grassland ecosystems, including interactions between livestock
and wild mammals (Michel and Overbeck, 2024). By contrast, central
and western regions of the country, including the Cerrado, Caatinga, and
Pantanal biomes, were notably underrepresented or absent in the
dataset. This likely reflects surveillance gaps rather than the true
absence of circulation. Despite the absence of deposited genetic se-
quences, Leptospira sp. has been previously molecularly and/or sero-
logically identified in animals and humans from these regions (Vieira
et al., 2016; Galan et al., 2023; Gomes et al., 2024; de Lisbˆoa Padilha
et al., 2025). These findings underscore a geographic and methodolog-
ical bias in available molecular data and emphasize the need to expand
and standardize surveillance efforts in understudied regions.
4.4. Environmental reservoirs and transmission cycles
Beyond hosts and geographic distribution, our dataset also revealed
the environmental component of Leptospira spp. transmission as a rele-
vant yet underexplored dimension (Table 1; Supplementary Material 1).
The identification of 44 sequences from environmental sources,
including puddles, sewage, soil, and freshwater, underscores the ability
of pathogenic Leptospira to persist in aquatic and semi‑aquatic envi-
ronments. Importantly, pathogenic leptospires are capable of forming
biofilms on abiotic surfaces and sediments, a trait that enhances
persistence by buffering cells against desiccation, UV exposure, nutrient
limitation, and antimicrobial stresses (Ristow et al., 2008; Meganathan
et al., 2022). Field investigations in Brazilian urban settings with poor
sanitation, particularly Salvador (Bahia), have repeatedly detected
pathogenic Leptospira in open sewers, floodwater, and street puddles
(Casanovas-Massana et al., 2020, 2022), supporting the role of envi-
ronmental matrices as maintenance and spillover interfaces for
rat‑borne leptospirosis where biofilm‑friendly conditions (moisture,
organic load, slightly alkaline pH) prevail (Bierque et al., 2020;
Davignon et al., 2023). Together, these experimental and field data
indicate that environmental reservoirs, potentially structured as bio-
films, play a crucial role in indirect transmission, especially in
flood‑prone urban areas and agricultural settings, where human and
animal exposure increases during rainfall or water accumulation. This
emphasize the importance of environmental management and infra-
structure improvements, such as sanitation, drainage, and flood-control
measures, to reduce environmental contamination and human exposure
in endemic areas.
To better illustrate the complex epidemiological scenario of lepto-
spirosis in Brazil, we developed a conceptual diagram (Fig. 3) repre-
senting the main transmission routes and host interfaces. The diagram
highlights the coexistence of distinct but interconnected cycles: (i) the
urban cycle, dominated by synanthropic rodents and dogs; (ii) the rural
and peri‑urban cycle, involving livestock, companion animals, and
humans in shared environments; and (iii) the wild cycle, where trans-
mission occurs among native wildlife species. All these cycles interact
dynamically through direct and indirect transmission routes, including
contact with contaminated environments and, in some cases, sexual
transmission. This multifaceted system reinforces the importance of
integrative approaches that consider ecological, socio-environmental,
and behavioral factors in leptospirosis surveillance and control.
To provide a visual synthesis of the main of the findings of the pre-
sent study, we developed an infographic summarizing the key genetic,
ecological, and geographic characteristics of pathogenic Leptospira spe-
cies circulating in Brazil, as detailed in the tables and results presented
above (Fig. 4).
5. Conclusions
This study provides the first nationwide, integrative molecular
overview of pathogenic Leptospira circulating across Brazilian biomes,
combining genetic, ecological, and epidemiological data from humans,
domestic animals, wildlife, and environmental sources. We revealed a
broad taxonomic and ecological host range, encompassing terrestrial,
arboreal, aquatic, synanthropic, and even non-mammalian taxa. While
the heterogeneous use of molecular markers and uneven geographic
coverage reveal important gaps in surveillance, the dataset and analyt-
ical framework presented here provide a valuable foundation for stan-
dardized molecular surveillance and for guiding targeted interventions
to reduce the burden of leptospirosis in tropical countries. It is important
to highlight that this marker heterogeneity may limit direct species
comparability and phylogenetic resolution and future studies should
aim to harmonize marker selection by adopting standardized genes,
such as secY and genome-wide approaches, which would enhance con-
sistency and enable more robust evolutionary and epidemiological in-
ferences across regions. The inclusion of environmental isolates further
reinforces the One Health perspective, underscoring the role of multiple
reservoirs and exposure pathways in leptospirosis epidemiology,
particularly under tropical conditions. Strengthening this integrative
approach will require coordinated surveillance and policy actions across
human, animal, and environmental health sectors, fostering data
sharing and early detection strategies to effectively mitigate leptospi-
rosis transmission.

ARTIGO 5: Diversidade genética e expansão clonal de Leptospira
patogênica no Brasil: um panorama multi-hospedeiro e multi-regional
Revista: Microorganisms (IF= 4.2)
A leptospirose é uma zoonose de distribuição global, de grande relevância para
a saúde pública e veterinária, causada por espécies patogênicas do gênero
Leptospira. O Brasil representa um local crítico de transmissão devido à sua
diversidade ecológica e às complexas interfaces hospedeiro -ambiente. Este
estudo explorou a diversidade e a estrutura genética de espécies patogênicas
de Leptospira spp. circulantes no Brasil por meio de uma análise de tip ificação
de sequência de locus único (SLST) baseada no gene secY. Um total de 531
sequências foram obtidas do GenBank e submetidas a análises filogenéticas e
de diversidade de haplótipos. A reconstrução por máxima verossimilhança
revelou clados fortemente suportados para sete espécies, sendo L. interrogans
a mais prevalente e amplamente distribuída entre hospedeiros e regiões. Essa
espécie apresentou evidências de expansão clonal, com um haplótipo dominante
(n = 242) compartilhado por humanos, animais domésticos e animais silvestres.
Em contraste, L. santarosai e L. noguchii exibiram alta diversidade haplotípica e
estruturas de rede reticuladas, refletindo maior variabilidade evolutiva. As
espécies L. kirschneri e L . borgpetersenii apresentaram variação haplotípica
reduzida, sendo a última associada principalmente ao gado, o que condiz com
seu perfil de adaptação ao hospedeiro. Redes de haplótipos baseadas em
hospedeiros e biomas revelaram tanto a ampla adaptabilidade ecológica de
certas linhagens quanto a presença exclusiva de haplótipos restritos a ambientes
específicos, como os encontrados em mamíferos marinhos do Oceano Atlântico.
Análises de distância genética confirmaram a forte resolução taxonômica do
gene secY, que distinguiu efetivamente espécies intimamente relacionadas, ao
mesmo tempo que capturou a diversid ade intraespecífica. Esses achados
fornecem uma visão molecular abrangente de leptospiras patogênicas no Brasil,
destacando a conectividade ecológica entre hospedeiros e biomas, bem como a
dinâmica evolutiva contrastante entre as espécies. Além de descreve r padrões
genéticos, nossas análises enfatizam processos evolutivos, conectividade
hospedeiro-ambiente e as implicações para a abordagem "Uma Só Saúde". Essa
estrutura integrativa fortalece a base para estratégias de vigilância e controle em
outras regiões endêmicas do mundo.

Abstract
Leptospirosis is a globally distributed zoonosis of major public health and veterinary
relevance, caused by pathogenic species of the genus Leptospira. Brazil is a hotspot for
transmission due to its ecological diversity and complex host–environment interfaces. This
study explored the genetic diversity and structure of circulating pathogenic Leptospira
spp. in Brazil through a single-locus sequence typing (SLST) analysis based on the secY
gene. A total of 531 sequences were retrieved from GenBank and subjected to phylogenetic
and haplotype diversity analyses. Maximum likelihood reconstruction revealed strongly
supported clades for seven species, with L. interrogans being the most prevalent and
broadly distributed across hosts and regions. This species showed evidence of clonal
expansion, with a dominant haplotype (n = 242) shared by humans, domestic animals, and
wildlife. In contrast, L. santarosai and L. noguchii exhibited high haplotypic diversity and
reticulated network structures, reﬂecting greater evolutionary variability. The species L.
kirschneri and L. borgpetersenii displayed reduced haplotypic variation, the latter mainly
associated with cattle, consistent with its host-adapted proﬁle. Host- and biome-based
haplotype networks revealed both the broad ecological adaptability of certain lineages and
the exclusive presence of haplotypes restricted to speciﬁc environments, such as those found
in marine mammals from the Atlantic Ocean. Genetic distance analyses conﬁrmed the
strong taxonomic resolution of the genesecY, which effectively distinguished closely related
species while capturing intraspeciﬁc diversity. These ﬁndings provide a comprehensive
molecular overview of pathogenic Leptospira in Brazil, highlighting ecological connectivity
across hosts and biomes, as well as the contrasting evolutionary dynamics among species.
Beyond describing genetic patterns, our analyses emphasize evolutionary processes, host–
environment connectivity, and the implications for One Health. This integrative framework
strengthens the basis for surveillance and control strategies in other endemic regions in
the world.

1. Introduction
Leptospirosis is a widespread zoonotic disease caused by pathogenic species of the
genus Leptospira, which circulate among multiple animal hosts and persist in diverse
ecological settings [ 1]. More than 160 mammalian species, along with several reptile
and amphibian species, have been identiﬁed as hosts or reservoirs of the bacteria. These

animals shed the pathogen primarily through urine, releasing it into the environment
and contaminating soil and water sources [ 2]. The primary route of human infection is
indirect, occurring when mucous membranes (eyes, mouth, nose) or abraded skin come
into contact with water, soil, or food contaminated by the urine of infected animals. Risk
is heightened in humid environments, during ﬂooding, or in waterlogged soils, which
enhance the survival and dissemination of leptospires, particularly in urban settings with
inadequate sanitation and high rodent densities [ 3]. Intense rainfall events can further
mobilize leptospires from soil into surface waters, thereby amplifying human exposure [4].
Given its complex transmission network involving humans, animals, and the environment,
leptospirosis exempliﬁes a quintessential One Health challenge, demanding integrated
surveillance and control strategies across sectors [5].
Globally, leptospirosis represents one of the most widespread zoonoses of bacterial
origin, with an estimated one million human cases annually and mortality exceeding
60,000 deaths per year. The disease burden is especially high in tropical countries of South
America and Southeast Asia, where climatic conditions favor environmental persistence
and host density is elevated [6]. Brazil represents one of the most important global hotspots
for leptospiral transmission due to its ecological heterogeneity and complex human–animal–
environment interfaces. The country encompasses six major biomes, Amazon, Atlantic
Forest, Cerrado, Caatinga, Pantanal, and Pampa, each harboring distinct climatic regimes,
wildlife communities, and anthropogenic pressures. This environmental mosaic provides
ideal conditions for the coexistence of multiple Leptospira species maintained by both wild
and domestic hosts [7]. In the country, human leptospirosis is endemic and often reaches
epidemic levels during the rainy season, particularly in capital cities and metropolitan
areas. Outbreaks are closely linked to ﬂooding, inadequate waste management, and high
rodent infestation, which together increase exposure in low-income communities. In rural
settings, occupational contact with livestock, contaminated water and soil represent major
risk factors [8]. Urban incidence is highest in the North and Northeast regions, whereas
rural cases predominate in the Southeast and South [9].
Leptospira remains a taxonomically complex and genetically diverse genus, encom-
passing more than 60 species that display a continuum of pathogenicity and ecological
adaptation [10]. Although several local studies have characterized Leptospira spp. from
speciﬁc hosts or regions in Brazil, comprehensive nationwide assessments integrating phy-
logenetic, ecological, and host data are still scarce. Most available information is fragmented
or limited to regional case studies, lacking a uniﬁed comparative framework across biomes.
Such integrative molecular analyses are essential to elucidate transmission pathways, assess
genetic variability within and between species, and understand the ecological connectivity
of circulating lineages. In this context, single-locus sequence typing (SLST) has proven to
be a particularly valuable approach, especially in situations where bacterial isolation is
unfeasible and only clinical samples are available. This technique relies on a single, highly
informative gene that provides sufﬁcient resolution for both genetic and phylogenetic
analyses and has already been successfully applied to other bacterial groups [11,12]. The
secY gene has emerged as one of the most informative loci for molecular detection and clas-
siﬁcation of pathogenic Leptospira. This housekeeping gene, which encodes a component of
the protein translocation channel, combines high interspeciﬁc variability with sufﬁcient con-
servation to allow ampliﬁcation from a wide range of clinical and environmental samples.
Its sequence polymorphism enables both species-level identiﬁcation and intraspeciﬁc differ-
entiation, while maintaining strong phylogenetic congruence with multilocus typing and
whole-genome approaches. Furthermore, the gene’s broad availability in public databases
facilitates large-scale comparative analyses and epidemiological surveillance [13,14].

In this study, we investigated the phylogenetic diversity and haplotype structure of
pathogenic Leptospira spp. in Brazil by analyzing sequences derived from human and
animal sources. By combining phylogenetic reconstruction, haplotype network inference,
and genetic distance analyses, we aimed to characterize species-level diversity, host and
biome associations, and evolutionary patterns of the main pathogenic taxa circulating in the
country. This integrative approach provides new insights into the molecular epidemiology
of Leptospira in a megadiverse tropical country and establishes a framework for One Health
surveillance and control strategies.
2. Materials and Methods
2.1. Data Collection and Curation
Nucleotide sequences were obtained from the NCBI GenBank repository using the
query “Leptospira AND Brazil AND secY” (accessed on 15 July 2025). We included only
sequences with conﬁrmed species-level identiﬁcation and available metadata regarding
host/source and geographic origin. Entries described solely as “ Leptospira sp.” without
species assignment were discarded, since accurate species identiﬁcation is essential for
molecular epidemiology analyses [15]. For this study, only pathogenic taxa belonging to
the P1 clade, as proposed [10], were retained, while intermediate and saprophytic species
were excluded. Each selected record was manually checked and annotated with key at-
tributes: GenBank accession, species name, strain or sample identiﬁer, host species, location
of identiﬁcation, and bibliographic reference. The curated dataset was organized in an
Excel spreadsheet.
To allow broader ecological and epidemiological interpretation, host species were
grouped into seven general categories: “Domestic large land animals”, “Wild land animals”,
“Pets”, “Humans”, “Marine mammals” and “Urban rodents”. Likewise, sampling sites
were assigned to one of the ﬁve main Brazilian biomes deﬁned by the Brazilian Institute of
Geography and Statistics (IBGE): Amazon, Atlantic Rain Forest, Pampa, Cerrado (Savanah),
and Caatinga (semi-arid), according to the original collection site. The Atlantic Ocean was
treated as a separate category (coastal-marine system, CMS).
2.2. Phylogenetic Analysis
Only secY sequences longer than 400 base pairs were retained to ensure reliable align-
ments and robust phylogenetic inference, as shorter fragments may reduce tree resolution
and inﬂate homoplasy. For genome-derived records, secY sequences were extracted using
the NCBI Genome Annotation tool, based on the corresponding GenBank or BioProject
accession numbers. All command-line analyses were performed using the WSL terminal
environment to ensure reproducibility and compatibility with bioinformatics tools. All
secY sequences corresponded to a partial fragment of the gene, covering approximately
positions 250–655 of the reference strain L. interrogans Fiocruz L1-130 (GenBank acces-
sion AE016823). After alignment and trimming, the ﬁnal analyzed fragment spanned
405 base pairs (bp).
Sequences were aligned using MAFFT v7.505 [ 16] with default settings. Phyloge-
netic reconstruction was performed using IQ-TREE v2.2.6 [17], applying the Tamura–Nei
(TN93) substitution model, as it was the best-ﬁtting DNA substitution model determined
by the Bayesian information criterion, with 1.000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates to assess
branch support. A bootstrap value of ≥70% was considered indicative of strong support.
The maximum likelihood (ML) tree generated was subsequently imported into MEGA X
v11.0.13 [18] for visualization and editing. Minor adjustments to tree layout, taxon labels,
and branch display were made to improve clarity and produce the ﬁnal version used for
interpretation and ﬁgure export.

2.3. Haplotype Networks
To further explore genetic patterns, median-joining haplotype networks were con-
structed using PopArt v1.7 using the median-joining inference method [19], based on the
aligned secY dataset for each Leptospira species. Two separate networks were generated:
one grouping haplotypes by host category and another by biome (as previously deﬁned).
Annotation was performed via a custom NEXUS input ﬁle to assign colors and groupings.
For single-locus analyses such as this, identical secY sequences were grouped into
unique haplotypes, deﬁned as sets of identical nucleotide sequences within the alignment.
The term “haplotype” is used here in its phylogenetic context to describe sequence clusters
derived from a single genetic locus, rather than the multilocus “sequence types (STs)” used
in conventional MLST schemes.
2.4. Estimation of Genetic Distances
To provide additional insights into the genetic cohesiveness of each species and the
degree of divergence between taxa occurring in Brazil, intraspeciﬁc and interspeciﬁc genetic
distances were calculated using MEGA X, based on the aligned secY sequences. Mean
pairwise distances within and between species were calculated under the TN93 model.
Standard error (SD) estimates were obtained by a bootstrap procedure (1000 replicates)
3. Results
3.1. Phylogenetic Relationships
A total of 531 sequences met the criteria and were included in the genetic analysis. Se-
lected sequences and associated information are shown in Supplementary Material Table S1.
The alignment spanned 405 bp, and the ML-TN93 tree recovered well-supported monophyletic
clades for each recognized species, with bootstrap values exceeding 90% for most nodes.
Notably ,L. interrogansshowed the highest number of total sequences and the greatest repre-
sentation across multiple hosts and regions (Figure 1 and Supplementary Material Table S1).
Moreover, it exhibited a remarkable clonal expansion represented by a predominant haplo-
type within the dataset comprising 242 sequences, including the reference strain Fiocruz
L1-130. Other frequent haplotypes within L. interrogans also contained 21 and 11 sequences.
Leptospira noguchii, L. kirschneri, and L. borgpetersenii showed less diversity of haplo-
types, with a predominance of one or two groups among 4 and 29 sequences, while L.
santarosai presented several haplotypes formed by a maximum of 5 sequences, as well
as presenting many unique sequences. The recently described species L. yasudae and L.
stimsonii were represented by fewer sequences, but still formed distinct clusters, clearly
indicating their genetic divergence from previously described species (Figure 1).
3.2. Haplotype Network Analysis by Host and Biome
The haplotype network based on L. interrogans sequences (Figure 2) revealed a total of
19 haplotypes, with one central haplotype comprising the majority of sequences (n = 242).
This predominant haplotype (Fiocruz L1-130-like group) included representatives from
several host categories, being practically equally distributed among humans, wild animals,
domestic large land animals, and dogs, with few urban rodents. Other larger haplotypes,
including about 20 sequences, are mostly from bovine origin. Small haplotypes, genetically
close to the larger ones, were formed by sequences from marine mammals, dogs, and wild
animals (Figure 2A).

For L. noguchii, the haplotype network exhibited a high degree of haplotypic diversity,
with several intermediate nodes and no single dominant haplotype. The sequences were
broadly distributed among multiple haplotypes, many of which were shared across host
categories. Domestic large land animals represented the majority of hosts, followed by
wild animals, humans, and dogs (Figure 3A). In the biome-speciﬁc network, haplotypes
were spread across three biomes, with notable abundance in the Atlantic Forest. Several
haplotypes were exclusive to a single biome, while two were shared across more regions
(Figure 3B).

Leptospira borgpetersenii also showed low haplotypic diversity, with a few dominant
haplotypes. The host haplotype network was formed almost exclusively by sequences
originating from cattle, with a single haplotype composed of an urban rodent sequence
(Figure 3E). In the biome-based network, sequences were predominantly from the Amazon,
followed by the Atlantic Forest. The urban rodent sequence was from the Pampa biome
(Figure 3F). Overall, the network structure was simpler compared to other species, with
fewer mutational steps and a more clustered organization.
The network for L. santarosai revealed the highest haplotypic diversity among the
species analyzed, with numerous haplotypes distributed along a reticulated and complex
structure. This network structure was characterized by multiple internal connections, and
no single haplotype was dominant. Host distribution showed dominance of domestic large
land animals and wild animals, with smaller contributions from dogs (Figure 3G). The
biome-based network was similarly diverse, with sequences from only two biomes, the
Atlantic Forest and Amazon, with only two shared between regions (Figure 3H).

3.3. Genetic Distances Within and Between Leptospira Species
Genetic distances (TN93) based on 531 nucleotide sequences of the secY gene revealed
low to moderate intraspeciﬁc variability across the ﬁve pathogenic Leptospira species circu-
lating in Brazil (bold values along the diagonal in Table 1). The lowest intraspeciﬁc distance
was observed for L. kirschneri (0.002), followed by L. noguchii (0.017) and L. interrogans
(0.004), while L. santarosai exhibited the highest intraspeciﬁc divergence (0.034). Regarding
interspeciﬁc comparisons (below the diagonal in Table 1), the smallest genetic distances
were found between L. interrogans, L. noguchii, and L. kirschneri (ranging from 0.02 to 0.03),
suggesting closer evolutionary relationships among these taxa. In contrast, L. borgpetersenii
and L. santarosai showed greater divergence in relation to the other species, with distances
reaching up to 0.24 when compared to L. noguchii. Standard deviations were generally low,
indicating consistency in pairwise comparisons (above diagonal in italics in Table 1).

4. Discussion
To explore the genetic structure of circulatingLeptospira spp. in Brazil, 531 secY gene
sequences were selected, a marker well established for both taxonomic and epidemiological
resolution [13,14]. This extensive dataset, encompassing sequences from multiple hosts and
biomes, provided a robust basis for investigating lineage diversiﬁcation and geographic
structuring at a national scale. Herein, thesecY locus has been consistently shown to balance
interspeciﬁc conservation with sufﬁcient intraspeciﬁc variability, allowing the reconstruc-
tion of reliable phylogenetic relationships while detecting microevolutionary signals within
populations. By combining secY-based phylogenetic reconstruction, haplotype network
analysis, and genetic distance estimation, we were able to delineate distinct evolutionary
clusters corresponding to recognized species and to visualize the degree of haplotypic
connectivity among hosts and regions.
The maximum likelihood phylogeny recovered strongly supported monophyletic
clades for each species, with L. interrogans showing the largest number of sequences and
broadest distribution across hosts and regions. This dominance underscores the remarkable
ecological versatility of L. interrogans, a species capable of maintaining stable transmission
cycles in both urban and rural settings, facilitated by its adaptability to a wide range of
mammalian hosts [20]. A striking feature was the evidence of clonal expansion, with a sin-
gle haplotype encompassing 242 sequences, including the reference strain Fiocruz L1-130,
detected in humans, domestic animals, and wildlife, and spanning multiple biomes. Such
extensive representation across hosts and regions indicates that this clone has achieved
ecological dominance, likely supported by its capacity to persist in both maintenance
and incidental hosts. The presence of identical sequences in geographically distant areas
also suggests recent or ongoing gene ﬂow among populations, possibly mediated by the
movement of livestock, companion animals, and synanthropic rodents. The success of this

lineage reﬂects both low genetic variability and wide ecological adaptability, consistent
with its role as the major cause of human outbreaks in Brazil, especially in urban centers
with high rodent infestation [21]. This evolutionary success likely results from a combina-
tion of host plasticity and environmental resilience, allowing the bacteria to survive under
ﬂuctuating conditions of humidity, temperature, and salinity. The lineage’s widespread
distribution also suggests a long-term evolutionary stability, possibly linked to efﬁcient
maintenance within rodent reservoirs and recurrent spillovers to other mammals. The
persistence of this haplotype across hosts and landscapes highlights its epidemiological
signiﬁcance: clonal stability may facilitate efﬁcient transmission, while reduced antigenic
diversity could simultaneously favor vaccine targeting and amplify risks of large-scale out-
breaks if this lineage continues to expand unchecked. From an epidemiological standpoint,
this pattern illustrates the dual nature of clonal expansion: it enhances predictability for
diagnostic and vaccine development yet increases vulnerability to epidemic resurgence
when environmental or climatic conditions become favorable for transmission. Continuous
genomic monitoring of this dominant haplotype could therefore serve as an early-warning
indicator for urban leptospirosis outbreaks. A clonal subpopulation of L. interrogans was
previously reported during leptospirosis outbreaks in Brazil [22]. Similarly, clonal expan-
sion of L. interrogans was identiﬁed as the predominant driver of leptospirosis cases in
the Indian archipelagos [23]. These ﬁndings, observed across independent epidemiolog-
ical settings, highlight a possible broader global trend in which a few highly adapted L.
interrogans lineages sustain the majority of human infections. Such convergence across
continents suggests evolutionary optimization toward transmission efﬁciency rather than
diversiﬁcation. However, further studies employing standardized genetic characterization
approaches are needed to conﬁrm this trend and elucidate its evolutionary and epidemio-
logical implications.
By contrast, L. kirschneri and L. borgpetersenii presented simpler network topologies,
with limited haplotypic variation and few mutational steps between clusters. The pre-
dominance of a small number of haplotypes may reﬂect host adaptation and reduced
environmental survival, particularly in the case of L. borgpetersenii, which has undergone
genome reduction and relies more on direct host-to-host transmission [24,25]. Recent ge-
nomic studies reinforce this restricted variability, showing that L. borgpetersenii lineages
circulating in cattle often cluster into very few haplotypes or STs, highlighting clonal
expansion and limited environmental persistence [26,27]. Similarly, L. kirschneri isolates
frequently display low genetic variability and well-structured clusters, consistent with
local host adaptation and geographically restricted lineages [28]. This restricted diversity is
consistent with their frequent association with cattle and other livestock, reinforcing the role
of domestic animals in maintaining adapted Leptospira lineages and shaping transmission
cycles [29].
Haplotype networks stratiﬁed by host and biome provided further resolution of phy-
logeographic patterns. For L. interrogans, the dominant haplotype was widely shared
among humans, cattle, dogs, and wildlife, and was particularly prevalent in the Atlantic
Forest biome. Such patterns corroborate previous ﬁndings of clonally dominant lineages
circulating in small mammals in this biome [30] and illustrate strong ecological connectivity
across hosts and environments. Shared haplotypes spanning different Brazilian biomes
emphasize lineage stability at continental scales, suggesting successful dispersal mech-
anisms possibly mediated by synanthropic reservoirs such as rodents. Similar patterns
have been documented elsewhere: in urban areas of Guangzhou, China, the coexistence
of L. interrogans, L. borgpetersenii, and L. kirschneri in commensal rodents was reported,
highlighting their role as long-term carriers and effective vehicles for dissemination across
ecological boundaries [31]. At the genomic level, Chinchilla and colleagues (2023) analyzed

914 genomes of L. santarosai from the Americas and revealed both region-speciﬁc clonal
groups and evidence of historical lineage movements across distant areas, pointing to
global-scale dispersal dynamics. Together, these ﬁndings suggest that haplotype sharing in
Brazil may not be an isolated phenomenon but rather part of a broader ecological and evo-
lutionary pattern in which synanthropic reservoirs facilitate the persistence and geographic
expansion of pathogenic Leptospira worldwide.
Exclusive haplotypes identiﬁed in marine mammals from the Atlantic Ocean expand
the ecological boundaries of leptospiral circulation. Although the genetic distances sepa-
rating these lineages were minimal (one to three substitutions), their exclusivity suggests
ecological isolation, with limited connectivity to terrestrial reservoirs. Nevertheless, the
zoonotic potential of this environment cannot be disregarded, as marine–terrestrial inter-
faces may represent overlooked transmission routes [32]. These ﬁndings reinforce the need
for frameworks that encompass both terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems..
The analysis of genetic distances supported the phylogenetic and haplotype network
results. Intraspeciﬁc distances were lowest for L. kirschneri (0.002) and L. interrogans (0.004),
consistent with clonal expansion and host-adapted transmission. By contrast, L. santarosai
showed the highest intraspeciﬁc divergence (0.034), reinforcing its evolutionary variability.
Interspeciﬁc distances indicated closer genetic relatedness among L. interrogans, L. noguchii,
and L. kirschneri, while L. borgpetersenii and L. santarosai were more distinct, a ﬁnding
consistent with whole-genome and cgMLST analyses [10,33,34]. Importantly, the absence of
overlap between maximum intraspeciﬁc and minimum interspeciﬁc distances underscores
the strong taxonomic resolution of secY, supporting its use as a robust marker for species
delimitation and intraspeciﬁc diversity assessment.
From a One Health perspective, the genetic connectivity observed among Leptospira
lineages circulating in humans, domestic animals, and wildlife underscores the importance
of coordinated surveillance across sectors. Molecular approaches such as secY-based typing
provide a practical and cost-effective tool to monitor pathogen ﬂow between hosts and en-
vironments, identify potential spillover interfaces, and guide preventive measures adapted
to local ecological contexts. By bridging molecular epidemiology with ecological data, this
study contributes to the integrated understanding required for sustainable leptospirosis
control in endemic tropical regions.
Despite these advances, some limitations should be considered. The reliance on
a single-locus marker, although informative, precludes the detection of recombination
events and ﬁne-scale genomic adaptations. Whole-genome approaches will be essential
to uncover hidden diversity and clarify evolutionary processes such as horizontal gene
transfer. Furthermore, sequence availability is uneven across hosts and regions, potentially
biasing haplotype frequencies and underrepresenting circulation in poorly sampled biomes
such as the Caatinga and Pantanal. Because the dataset analyzed here was entirely derived
from publicly available secY sequences, it reﬂects the representativeness of deposited
records rather than the true prevalence of genotypes in nature. The apparent predominance
of certain haplotypes may therefore result from uneven research efforts, regional sampling
preferences, or repeated sequencing of epidemiologically important isolates. Consequently,
the patterns described in this study should be interpreted as indicators of genetic diversity
and connectivity within the available dataset, not as estimates of infection frequency or
epidemiological dominance. Finally, future studies combining Brazilian and international
datasets will be essential to determine whether the country harbors unique endemic clades
or mainly reﬂects the global diversity structure of pathogenic Leptospira. In this context,
formal nomenclature ofsecY-based haplotypes should be pursued to facilitate comparability
among research groups and ensure consistent lineage recognition across regions worldwide.

Addressing these gaps through coordinated sampling efforts will be critical for a truly
comprehensive picture of Leptospira diversity in Brazil and in the world.
5. Conclusions
This study provides a comprehensive molecular overview of the genetic diversity of
pathogenic Leptospira circulating in Brazil. Phylogenetic analyses based on the secY gene
revealed well-supported clades for the main pathogenic species, while haplotype network
analyses uncovered contrasting evolutionary patterns, ranging from clonal expansion in L.
interrogans to extensive haplotypic diversity in L. santarosai and L. noguchii. Host and biome-
based networks highlighted both the ecological adaptability of dominant lineages and the
existence of exclusive haplotypes in speciﬁc environments, such as marine mammals in the
Atlantic Ocean. Genetic distance estimates conﬁrmed the strong taxonomic resolution of
secY, distinguishing closely related species while capturing intraspeciﬁc diversity. Together,
these ﬁndings conﬁrm the complex interplay of host, environment, and pathogens shaping
leptospiral diversity. By bridging phylogenetics with ecological and epidemiological
contexts, this work contributes to a deeper understanding of leptospiral transmission
dynamics and provides a valuable framework for One Health surveillance and control
strategies in endemic regions.

DISCUSSÃO
O presente estudo apresenta um panorama inédito sobre a diversidade
genética de leptospiras patogênicas circulantes no Brasil, integrando dados de
múltiplos hospedeiros e regiões. Essa abordagem permitiu caracterizar as
estirpes em nível genético, inferir padrões de circulação e rotas de transmissão,
além de elucidar o potencial zoonótico das linhagens identificadas.
A alta identidade genética entre estirpes isoladas de cães e humanos
confirma a estreita interface zoonóti ca entre essas populações, sugerindo que
os cães atuam não apenas como sentinelas, mas também como amplificadores
da infecção em áreas urbanas e periurbanas, mesmo quando assintomáticos
(Sant’Anna et al., 2017; Sant’Anna et al., 2021). Em diferentes reg iões da
América do Sul, a soroprevalência canina varia de 18% a 20%, sendo mais
elevada em animais com acesso à rua, oriundos de áreas de vulnerabilidade
social e com maior exposição a ambientes contaminados, presença de roedores
e contato com água ou solo úmido (Esteves et al., 2023; Ricardo et al., 2024;
Griebsch et al., 2025). Cães errantes, filhotes, machos e idosos também
apresentam risco aumentado (Griebsch et al., 2025). Em canis, surtos podem
ocorrer mesmo em animais vacinados , devido à circulação d e sorogrupos não
contemplados nas vacinas comerciais, reforçando a necessidade de vigilância
contínua (Miotto et al., 2018; Balboni et al., 2022).
A transmissão direta de cães para humanos é possível, sobretudo pelo
contato com urina de animais infectados, havendo relatos de casos humanos
associados a surtos caninos (Azócar -Aedo e Monti, 2022; Balboni et al., 2022;
Guzmán et al., 2023; Ricardo et al., 2024), inclusive em regiões de baixo risco,
como Wyomin g, EUA (Waranius et al., 2024), onde o aumento da va cinação
canina foi associado à redução do risco para humanos expostos. Em regiões
tropicais, cães utilizados em atividades de caça apresentam alta soroprevalência
e podem atuar como sentinelas para os humanos envolvidos nessas práticas
(Orr et al., 2022), reforçando seu papel como elo entre ambientes silvestres e
domésticos. Esses achados reforçam o papel importante dos cães na
epidemiologia da leptospirose e destacam a importância de incluir esses animais

88



em programas integrados de vigilância e controle, especialmente em
comunidades vulneráveis com alta circulação de roedores.
Nos bovinos, observou-se epidemiologia distinta dos cães, marcada pela
predominância de L. borgpetersenii e L. interrogans do sorogrupo Sejroe,
sobretudo em infecções genitais crônic as. A detecção de haplótipos exclusivos
do trato reprodutivo, não compartilhados com estirpes renais, sugere adaptação
dessas leptospiras ao ambiente genital bovino. Foi recentemente demonstrado
que estirpes de L. santarosai isoladas de trato genital apres entam adaptações
genômicas específicas que favorecem colonização e persistência nesse nicho
(Di Azevedo et al., 2025). Evidências moleculares confirmam a presença de
leptospiras em tecidos genitais mesmo na ausência de excreção urinária
detectável (Aymée et al., 2021), consolidando o conceito de leptospirose genital
bovina e expondo as limitações dos métodos sorológicos tradicionais para
detectar infecções silenciosas. Essa forma subclínica e crônica representa
desafio significativo à saúde animal e públ ica, pois facilita a disseminação
silenciosa no rebanho e no ambiente (Loureiro e Lilenbaum, 2020; Aymée et al.,
2024; Barnabé et al., 2024). A detecção de leptospiras em fluidos genitais e
sêmen (Maiolino et al., 2021; Pedrosa et al., 2024) aponta para um a rota de
transmissão venérea ainda subexplorada. Tal via pode comprometer a eficiência
reprodutiva e ampliar o risco de exposição humana, sobretudo entre
trabalhadores rurais e inseminadores, que manipulam secreções contendo
leptospiras viáveis (Alinaitwe et al., 2019; Mai et al., 2021). Espécies do
sorogrupo Sejroe já foram isoladas de casos humanos (Romero e Yasuda, 2006;
Kakita et al., 2020), evidenciando seu potencial zoonótico e a necessidade de
vigilância sanitária que inclua testes moleculares e vacinação com cepas locais.
A ausência de obrigatoriedade de notificação da leptospirose animal em países
como o Brasil contribui para subnotificação e lacunas críticas na vigilância
integrada, contrariando os princípios da abordagem Uma Só Saúde.
Já a análise de pequenos mamíferos silvestres na Mata Atlântica revelou
ampla circulação de L. interrogans com haplótipos idênticos à estirpe Fiocruz L1-
130, indicando intensa atividade zoonótica mesmo em ecossistemas
preservados. Essa homogeneidade genética reflete a plasticidade ecológica de

89



clones epidêmicos capazes de se adaptar a diferentes nichos e hospedeiros. A
positividade observada (56%) está em consonância com achados prévios na
região (Vieira et al., 2019a, 2019b). Em áreas rurais do mesmo bioma, foram
registradas menores prevalências (21,3%) e menor diversidade de hospedeiros
(Silva et al., 2023), o que é esperado, uma vez que as áreas de conservação
tendem a sustentar maior diversidade e abundância de reservatórios, maior
persistência ambiental da bact éria e redes tróficas mais estáveis, além de
apresentarem uso reduzido de medidas de controle e menor competição com
espécies sinantrópicas (Bradley e Lockaby, 2023). Por outro lado, a degradação
da Mata Atlântica, que atualmente mantém apenas 12,4% de sua cobertura
original (Ribei ro et al., 2023), intensifica o contato entre humanos, animais
domésticos e silvestres, elevando o risco de transmissão de doenças zoonóticas.
Fatores como fragmentação de habitat, alterações tróficas, aumento da
exposição a águas contaminadas e mudanças climáticas contribuem para a
persistência e disseminação de leptospiras (Pfenning-Butterworth et al., 2024).
De uma forma geral, a compilação de 825 sequências obtidas entre 2009
e 2025 de origem humana e animais domésticos, sinantrópicos e silvestres
constitui o conjunto molecular mais abrangente de Leptospira spp. no Brasil,
evidenciando o avanço das ferramentas genéticas na vigilância do patógeno.
Embora a diversidade de espécies patog ênicas seja conhecida ( Pyskun e
Richter, 2025 ), a predominância de L. interrogans (74,9%) reforça seu papel
como principal agente infeccioso global (Rajapakse et al., 2025) e no Brasil
(Albuquerque et al., 2017a; Jorge et al., 2018; Paz et al., 2019; Sique ira et al.,
2020; Gomes et al., 2022; Freitas et al., 2024). Outras espécies, como L.
santarosai, L. borgpetersenii, L. noguchii e L. kirschneri foram detectadas com
menor frequência (3 –10%), o que pode refletir não apenas subnotificação ou
desigualdade na vigilância molecular entre regiões, mas também diferenças
ecológicas e adaptativas, uma vez que essas espécies tendem a apresentar
nichos mais restritos, menor capacidade de persistência ambiental ou menor
eficiência de transmissão em comparação a L. interrogans.
A predominância de L. interrogans em ambientes urbanos confirma sua
adaptação a ciclos sinantrópicos envolvendo roedores e cães (Bradley e

90



Lockaby, 2023), enquanto L. borgpetersenii, L. kirschneri e L. noguchii são mais
frequentes em áreas rurais, associadas a hospedeiros domésticos e silvestres
(Guedes et al., 2019; Soares et al., 2020). Leptospira santarosai, distribuída entre
zonas rurais e periurbanas, apresenta flexibilidade ecológica e potencial de
sobreposição entre ciclos silvestres e domés ticos (Chinchilla et al., 2023). Essa
heterogeneidade reflete o papel da paisagem na circulação das leptospiras,
embora os dados devam ser interpretados com cautela, pois resultam de
esforços amostrais desiguais entre regiões e hospedeiros.
Do ponto de vis ta taxonômico, foram identificadas 78 espécies
hospedeiras, incluindo duas classes (mamíferos e répteis) de 12 ordens
distintas. Destas, as mais notáveis foram Artiodactyla (mamíferos ungulados,
como ruminantes e suínos), Rodentia (roedores), Carnivora (pr incipalmente
cães) e Primates (humanos). Essa diversidade reforça o conceito clássico de
leptospirose como uma zoonose multihospedeira, na qual os ciclos de
transmissão são mantidos por uma ampla variedade de espécies com diferentes
funções epidemiológicas (Belsare et al., 2022).
Leptospira interrogans apresentou ampla distribuição geográfica,
ocorrendo em todos os biomas e paisagens. As regiões Sudeste e Sul
concentraram o maior número de registros e riqueza de espécies, provavelmente
devido à maior infraestrutura de pesquisa e às condições ambientais favoráveis
à transmissão, como inundações frequentes e infestação por roedores (Nardoni
Marteli et al., 2022; Michelon et al., 2025). A Mata Atlântica destacou-se como o
principal hotspot de Leptospira, seguida pela Amazônia, enquanto o Cerrado, a
Caatinga e Pantanal permanecem sub-representados, apesar das evidências de
circulação previamente documentadas por detecções moleculares e sorológicas
em animais e humanos (Vieira et al., 2016; Galan et al., 2023; Lisbôa Padilha et
al., 2025).
A presença de 44 sequências ambientais (poças, esgoto, solo, água doce)
evidencia a importância das matrizes ambientais na persistência e transmissão
de Leptospira. A capacidade de formar biofilmes em superfícies abióticas confere
resistência e sobrevivência prolongada (Ristow et al., 2008; Meganathan et al.,
2022). Estudos brasileiros em áreas urbanas com saneamento precário

91



confirmam a detecção recorrente de Leptospira patogênicas em esgoto e águas
pluviais (Casanovas -Massana e t al., 2020, 2022), reforçando o papel do
ambiente como interface de manutenção e transbordamento (Bierque et al.,
2020; Davignon et al., 2023).
A análise de 531 sequências do gene secY revelou cinco espécies
patogênicas principais e forte expansão clonal de L. interrogans, com haplótipo
dominante incluindo à estirpe Fiocruz L1-130. Essa linhagem, associada a surtos
urbanos e infestação por roedores (Jaeger et al., 2018), apresentou baixa
variabilidade genética e alta adaptabilidade ecológica. Leptospira borgpetersenii
e L. kirschneri exibiram baixa diversidade haplotípica e restrição geográfica,
compatíveis com adaptação ao hospedeiro e menor sobrevivência ambiental
(Bulach et al., 2006; Picardeau et al., 2008; Aymée et al., 2022; Benvin et al.,
2025).
As r edes haplotípicas mostraram haplótipos compartilhados entre
diversos hospedeiros, com destaque para humanos, cães, bovinos e mamíferos
silvestres, com maior ocorrência na Mata Atlântica. O compartilhamento entre
biomas indica estabilidade genética e dispersão mediada por reservatórios
sinantrópicos, padrão também observado em roedores urbanos na Ásia (Shao
et al., 2022). Haplótipos exclusivos detectados em mamíferos mar inhos do
Atlântico, embora geneticamente próximos aos terrestres (1 –3 substituições),
indicam isolamento ecológico e possíveis rotas marinho -terrestres de
transmissão negligenciadas, o que reforça a importância de abordagens que
integrem ecossistemas terrestres e aquáticos (Torres et al., 2025).
A análise das distâncias genéticas confirmou os padrões observados na
filogenia e nas redes haplotípicas. As menores divergências intraespecíficas
foram registradas para L. kirschneri (0.002) e L. interrogans (0.004), refletindo
expansão clonal e adaptação ao hospedeiro, enquanto L. santarosai apresentou
maior variabilidade (0.034). As distâncias interespecíficas revelaram maior
proximidade entre L. interrogans, L. noguchii e L. kirschneri, e maior distinção de
L. borgpetersenii e L. santarosai, em concordância com análises genômicas e de
cgMLST (Vincent et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2016; Guglielmini et al., 201). A ausência

92



de sobreposição entre distâncias intra e interespecíficas reforça a alta resolução
taxonômica do gene secY como marcador para delimitação de espécies.
A conectividade genética observada entre linhagens de Leptospira em
humanos, animais domésticos e silvestres reforça a necessidade de vigilância
integrada entre setores. Abordagens moleculares baseadas n o gene secY são
ferramentas eficazes e de baixo custo para monitorar o fluxo do patógeno,
identificar interfaces de transbordamento e orientar medidas preventivas
adaptadas aos contextos ecológicos locais. O uso de um único marcador,
entretanto, limita a d etecção de recombinações e adaptações genômicas.
Estudos amplos baseados em sequenciamento de genoma completo são
essenciais para revelar diversidade oculta e processos evolutivos, como
transferência horizontal de genes. Além disso, a desigualdade amostral entre
hospedeiros e regiões pode enviesar frequências haplotípicas, especialmente
em biomas pouco amostrados. Como o conjunto analisado baseou -se em
registros públicos, os padrões refletem a representatividade dos dados
depositados, e não necessariamente a prevalência real. Futuros estudos
integrando bancos brasileiros e internacionais serão fundamentais para verificar
se o país abriga clados endêmicos ou reflete a estrutura global de diversidade
de Leptospira. A adoção de uma nomenclatura formal para haplótipos baseados
em secY será igualmente crucial para padronizar comparações entre grupos de
pesquisa e regiões.

CONCLUSÕES
 As análises in silico de sequências de Leptospira spp. associadas à
infecção canina na América Latina evidenciaram baixa variabilidade
genética e ampla distribuição geográfica de linhagens clonais, reforçando
o papel dos cães como hospedeiros sentinelas na vigilância da
leptospirose.

 A detecção molecular em amostras reprodutivas de bovinos do Sudeste
brasileiro confirmou a circulação de Leptospira spp. patogênicas
associadas à forma crônica da leptospirose bovina, destac ando a

93



relevância do trato genital como sítio de manutenção e persistência do
patógeno.

 A caracterização genética de Leptospira spp. em pequenos mamíferos da
Mata Atlântica revelou elevada diversidade de espécies e haplótipos,
evidenciando o papel desses reservatórios silvestres na manutenção
ecológica do agente e seu potencial zoonótico.

 A integração de sequências provenientes de diferentes genes,
hospedeiros e biomas permitiu identificar padrões ecoepidemiológicos
consistentes de circulação de Leptospira spp. patogênicas no Brasil, sob
a perspectiva Uma Só Saúde.

 As análises filogenéticas e de diversidade genética indicaram
heterogeneidade evolutiva entre as espécies circulantes, com evidências
de expansão clonal em algumas linhagens e maior estruturação genética
em outras, refletindo processos de adaptação a hospedeiros e ambientes
distintos.

iv



























Dedico este trabalho a minha avó Miriam, cuja fé na educação
acendeu minha própria vocação. Pedagoga, com sua mente
paciente, alfabetizou -me. Com seu olhar além do tempo,
mostrou-me o caminho da pesquisa e da docência.

v


AGRADECIMENTOS

À Universidade Federal Fluminense, instituição que me acolheu em difer entes fases
da vida acadêmica, como graduanda, pós -doutoranda e, agor a, doutoranda pela
segunda vez, deixo minha gratidão mais profunda. Foi na UFF que dei meus primeiros
passos na ciência, amadureci como pesquisadora e encontrei propósito no que faço.
Sempre será meu lar acadêmico e afetivo. Levo comigo um pedaço dela, e deixarei
espalhadas, por todos os caminhos que ainda passarei , as sementes do que vivi e
aprendi aqui.

Ao Programa de Pós -Graduação em Microbiologia e Parasitologia Aplicadas, por ter
me recebido de braços abertos nessa nova aventura científica. Sou profundamente
grata aos professores que se tornaram amigos, e, agora, colegas de profissão, pelos
ensinamentos, pelas trocas e pelas inspi rações. Em especial, aos coordenadores
Ricardo Machado e Andrea Baptista, pela paciência, compreensão e apoio constante,
que fizeram toda diferença no percurso.

Às agências de fomento, FAPERJ e CNPq, pelo suporte financeiro que tornou possível
a execução do projeto e a fluidez da pesquisa.

Ao meu orientador, Prof. Walter Lilenbaum, por ter sido o grande alicerce desta
jornada. Sob sua orientação, aprendi mais do que técnicas novas e conceitos, aprendi
sobre rigor científico e paixão pela pesquisa. Costum o dizer que entrei como uma
recém-doutora e saí pesquisadora. Literalmente, pois foi aprovada, nesse período, em
três concursos públicos. Foi uma honra e um privilégio trilhar esse caminho ao lado
de um pesquisador de excelência.

Ao meu amigo Walter Lilen baum, com quem desde o início compartilhei afinidades
que ultrapassaram a esfera acadêmica. Segurou minha mão não apenas para
escrever artigos, mas também nos momentos em que a vida pesou. Choramos, rimos
e celebramos juntos em diversos momentos, sejam ele s triviais ou marcantes . Mais
uma vez, a UFF me deu mais que um título, me deu um grande amigo.

vi


À minha companheira de bancada e de vida científica, Luiza Aymée, meu braço direito
em tantos experimentos, coletas e discussões. Partilhamos vitórias, frustraç ões e
cafés intermináveis. Sua dedicação e amizade foram combustível diário, e é uma
alegria vê-la, agora, também seguir seu caminho na docência.

Às minhas queridas alunas de iniciação científica, Ana Luiza Borges, Luiza Reis, Ana
Clara Soares e Camila Ezepha, que mergulharam comigo nos desafios do laboratório,
enfrentando longos dias de coleta, experimentos e aprendizado. Este trabalho é
também fruto do esforço e entusiasmo de vocês. E como é gratificante ver vocês
seguindo um caminho brilhante.

A todas as demais colegas que fizeram do LaBV/UFF minha segunda casa por sete
anos, Juliana Lória, Juliana Pedrosa, Isabel Soares e Julia Mendes. Obrigada por cada
conversa, cada risada, cada dado analisado em conjunto. A ciência se faz em equipe,
e eu tive a sorte de ter a melhor ao meu lado.

À minha família e meus amigos , que mais uma vez acreditaram nos meus sonhos,
mesmo quando pareciam um delírio. Um segundo doutorado? Pois é. Aparentemente
improvável, mas necessário. E eles estiveram lá, orgulhosos, firme s, aplaudindo a
cada nova etapa concluída.

À minha esposa, Danielle, que foi a primeira a dizer “vai, que eu te apoio. Se der certo,
serei a primeira a te abraçar. Se der errado , também”. Quando tudo ainda era uma
ideia incerta e distante, ela se fez luz para minha decisão . Esteve comigo em cada
passo, segurou minha mão nos momentos difíceis e me lembrou, com amor e lucidez,
que vale a pena correr atrás dos sonhos.

Fazer um segundo doutorado não foi uma escolha fácil, mas foi a escolha certa: a que
me trouxe até aqui. Mais madura, mais consciente e pronta para um novo capítulo da
minha vida. Encerro esta etapa com o coraçã o cheio de aprendizado e afeto. Levo
comigo não apenas uma tese, mas uma história de crescimento pessoal e superação
que sempre me lembrará que o impossível só existe para quem desiste de tentar.

vii




























“Devemos acreditar que somos talentosas para
alguma coisa, e que essa coisa, a qualquer
custo, deve ser alcançada”

Marie Curie

viii


RESUMO

A leptospirose é uma doença negligenciada de ampla distribuição no Brasil, com
impacto significativo na saúde pública. Diante do aumento das zoonoses associadas
às mudanças ambientais e climáticas, a doença permanece como um desafio
emergente, exigindo uma compreensão mais profun da de seus padrões de
transmissão e da diversidade genética dos agentes envolvidos. Este estudo teve como
objetivo investigar a diversidade genética, as relações evolutivas e os padrões de
circulação de Leptospira spp. patogênicas no Brasil, a partir de diferentes
hospedeiros, regiões geográficas e fontes ambientais. Para isso, foram integradas
abordagens moleculares in vitro e in silico, incluindo diagnóstico por PCR, tipificação
baseada no gene secY, análises filogenéticas e de rede haplotípica, além da curadoria
e compilação de extensos bancos de dados genéticos e metadados ecológicos. As
análises integradas evidenciaram ampla diversidade ecológica de Leptospira spp.
patogênicas, geneticamente identificadas prin cipalmente em ruminantes, cães,
humanos e pequenos mamíferos silvestres. De forma importante, também foram
identificadas em amostras ambientais. Mata Atlântica e Amazônia foram os biomas
com maior número de ocorrências. Essa elevada diversidade detectada e ntre
múltiplos hospedeiros e biomas evidencia a complexa estrutura ecoepidemiológica da
leptospirose no país. A espécie mais frequente foi L. interrogans , seguida por L.
santarosai, L. borgpetersenii, L. kirschneri e L. noguchii . Observou-se ampla
sobreposição genética entre estirpes de diferentes origens e a predominância de um
haplótipo clonal de L. interrogans do sorogrupo Icterohaemorrhagiae, amplamente
disseminado. Essa homogeneidade genética indica a consolidação de um ciclo de
transmissão sustentado por reservatórios sinantrópicos e pela intensa interação entre
espécies e ambientes. Tais evidências revelam a forte interconexão entre os ciclos
urbano, rural e silvestre e confirmam o papel de animais domésticos, silvestres e do
ambiente como fontes potenciais de infecção humana. De forma integrada, os
resultados destacam a importância de incorporar ferramentas de epidemiologia
molecular à vigilância e ao controle, fortalecendo uma abordagem efetivamente One
Health (Uma só saúde) para o enfrentamento da leptospirose no Brasil.

ABSTRACT

Leptospirosis is a neglected zoonosis with a wide distribution in Brazil, having a
significant impact on public health. Given the increase in zoonoses associated with
environmental and climatic changes, the disease remains an emerging challenge,
requiring a deeper understanding of its transmission patterns and the genetic diversity
of the agents involved. This study aimed to investigate the genetic diversity,
evolutionary relationships, and circulation patterns of pathogenic Leptospira spp. in
Brazil, from different hosts, geographic regions, and environmental sources. To this
end, in vitro and in silico molecular app roaches were integrated, including PCR
diagnosis, secY gene-based typing, phylogenetic and haplotype network analyses, as
well as the curation and compilation of extensive genetic databases and ecological
metadata. The integrated analyses revealed a wide ecological diversity of pathogenic
Leptospira spp., genetically identified mainly in ruminants, dogs, humans, and small
wild mammals. Importantly, they were also identified in environmental samples. The
Atlantic Forest and Amazon biomes had the highest number of occurrences. This high
diversity detected among multiple hosts and biomes highlights the complex eco -
epidemiological structure of leptospirosis in the country. The most frequent species
was L. interrogans, followed by L. santarosai, L. borgpetersenii, L. kirschneri, and L.
noguchii. Extensive genetic overlap was observed between strains of different origins,
and a clonal haplotype of L. interrogans from the widely disseminated serogroup
Icterohaemorrhagiae predominated. This genetic homogeneity indica tes the
consolidation of a transmission cycle sustained by synanthropic reservoirs and the
intense interaction among species and environments. Such evidence reveals the
strong interconnection between urban, rural, and sylvatic cycles and confirms the role
of domestic, wild, and domestic animals as potential sources of human infection. Taken
together, the results highlight the importance of incorporating molecular epidemiology
tools into surveillance and control, strengthening an effectively One Health appro ach
to tackling leptospirosis in Brazil.
